meta.blurb: Neanderthals, Denisovans and our own species once shared the world, and now only one is left. This book follows the story of Homo sapiens, from the first stone tools to the Moon and a world of eight billion people.
meta.bible:
Homo sapiens: our own species, which appeared in Africa at least 300,000 years ago; every person alive today belongs to it. Neanderthals: a human species of Europe and Western Asia, died out about 40,000 years ago. Denisovans: another human species, known mostly from bones and teeth found in Siberia and Tibet. Homo erectus, Homo floresiensis: other human species. Places: Africa, Morocco, Europe, Asia, Israel, Australia, Indonesia, Flores, Siberia, Alaska, Americas, Fertile Crescent, Middle East, China, Mexico, New Guinea, Turkey, Mesopotamia, Uruk, Babylon, Egypt, Nile, Giza, Indus, Persia, Lydia, Rome, Baghdad, Germany, Britain, Atlantic, Jupiter, Moon, Mississippi. People: Hammurabi: king of Babylon about 3,700 years ago. Khufu: the pharaoh who built the Great Pyramid. Confucius, the Buddha, Socrates: thinkers of about 2,500 years ago. Johannes Gutenberg: printer of Germany, about 1450. Christopher Columbus: sailed in 1492. Galileo: used a telescope in 1610. Isaac Newton: published his laws in 1687. Edward Jenner: used a safe injection against smallpox in 1796. Fritz Haber and Carl Bosch: German chemists who found how to make fertiliser from air. Wilbur and Orville Wright: flew in 1903. Yuri Gagarin: first person in space, 1961. Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin: first on the Moon, 1969. chapters: The Long Way Out of Africa

beats.scene: A small group of people look out over a wide plain at sunrise
beats.summary: Humans are one species among millions, yet we have changed the whole planet; this book follows the journey from a small group in Africa to a world of eight billion.

beats.scene: Planet Earth turning slowly in black space beside a bright sun
beats.summary: Earth is about four and a half billion years old, and our species arrived only in the last few seconds of its story.

beats.scene: Small furry animals scurry beneath tall ferns under a glowing red sky
beats.summary: After the dinosaurs died out about 66 million years ago, small mammals spread across the world.

beats.scene: A small monkey grips a branch high in a green forest tree
beats.summary: Primates, the group of mammals that includes monkeys and apes, have gripping hands and forward-looking eyes.

beats.scene: A chimpanzee mother and her baby sit together under tall forest trees
beats.summary: Humans are apes, and our closest living relatives are the chimpanzees and bonobos.

beats.scene: Apes in an African forest at the edge of a spreading grassland
beats.summary: Humans and chimpanzees share an ancestor that lived in Africa about six to seven million years ago.

beats.scene: Two lines of footprints cross a layer of grey volcanic ash
beats.summary: At Laetoli in Tanzania, early human relatives left footprints in volcanic ash more than three and a half million years ago, showing that they walked upright.

beats.scene: An early human relative stands tall in grass, looking far across the plain
beats.summary: Walking on two legs may have saved energy and gave early humans free hands; scientists still debate why it began.

beats.scene: Scientists in a hot dusty valley kneel beside small fossil bones
beats.summary: In 1974 scientists in Ethiopia found Lucy, a small upright walker who lived about three million years ago.

beats.scene: Hands strike one stone against another to make a sharp flake
beats.summary: By about two and a half million years ago, our relatives were breaking stones into sharp flakes to cut meat and crack bones.

beats.scene: A small early human with a rounded head examines a stone tool
beats.summary: Around two to three million years ago the first members of our own group, Homo, appeared in Africa, with bigger brains than Lucy's.

beats.scene: A tall boy with long legs strides through dry grass under a hot sky
beats.summary: Homo erectus, who appeared nearly two million years ago, was tall, long-legged and built for walking great distances.

beats.scene: Hands chip both sides of a teardrop-shaped stone into a sharp axe
beats.summary: Homo erectus made hand axes by chipping both sides of a stone, a design that stayed in use for over a million years.

beats.scene: A small group of early people walk across hills in a new land
beats.summary: Homo erectus were the first humans to leave Africa, reaching western Asia, Java and China.

beats.scene: People sit in a circle around a crackling fire in a dark cave
beats.summary: At some point our ancestors learned to control fire, giving warmth, light and protection; scientists disagree about when.

beats.scene: Firelight glows on faces and sharpened sticks as night falls
beats.summary: Fire kept animals away, lengthened the day, and could harden the tips of wooden spears.

beats.scene: A person turns a piece of meat over hot stones beside a fire
beats.summary: Cooking made food softer and easier to digest, and may have helped to feed the energy-hungry human brain.

beats.scene: A mother holds a baby while an older girl and an old woman watch
beats.summary: Human brains grew about three times larger, and helpless babies needed years of care, so people shared the work of raising children.

beats.scene: Hunters in a misty marsh raise long wooden spears towards wild horses
beats.summary: About 300,000 years ago hunters at Schöningen in Germany made fine wooden throwing spears and hunted horses together.

beats.scene: One group in snowy Europe, another in warm Africa, living far apart
beats.summary: By about 300,000 years ago descendants of earlier humans had split into separate groups in Africa and Europe, which would become us and the Neanderthals.

beats.scene: Early humans with rounded skulls stand outside a cave in the Moroccan hills
beats.summary: Our species, Homo sapiens, appeared in Africa at least 300,000 years ago; its oldest known bones come from Jebel Irhoud in Morocco.

beats.scene: Different groups of early people live in distant parts of the African landscape
beats.summary: Other early Homo sapiens fossils from Ethiopia and South Africa suggest that our species grew from groups all over Africa, not from one place.

beats.scene: A broad, stocky Neanderthal hunter walks through snow with a spear
beats.summary: Neanderthals were strong, stocky people who lived in Europe and western Asia for hundreds of thousands of years and had brains as big as ours.

beats.scene: A Neanderthal family sits beside a fire in a cold, snowy landscape
beats.summary: Neanderthals made fire, spears, clothing and glue, and cared for the sick and injured.

beats.scene: A Neanderthal hand presses red paint onto a cave wall
beats.summary: A few finds hint that Neanderthals made ornaments and marks, but scientists still argue about what they meant.

beats.scene: A scientist holds a tiny finger bone inside a Siberian cave
beats.summary: In 2010 DNA from a finger bone found in Denisova Cave in Siberia revealed a new human group, the Denisovans.

beats.scene: A tiny adult person stands beside a giant rat on a tropical island
beats.summary: On the island of Flores in Indonesia lived a small human, nicknamed the hobbit, until about 50,000 years ago.

beats.scene: Scientists crawl through a narrow passage into a deep dark cave
beats.summary: In South Africa, a small-brained human called Homo naledi lived about the same time as the first Homo sapiens.

beats.scene: Travellers carry shiny black stones and red powder across an open plain
beats.summary: In East Africa, stones and pigments were carried long distances about 300,000 years ago, a sign that groups were in touch.

beats.scene: Several faces of different human species lined up side by side
beats.summary: For most of its history our species shared the world with other kinds of human, and nobody is sure what made us the survivors.

beats.scene: A small band of people camp beside a river, sharing out roots and meat
beats.summary: For almost all of history people lived in small bands of a few dozen, moving with the seasons to find food.

beats.scene: Women and men dig roots and carry spears across a wide valley
beats.summary: Foragers gathered plants and hunted animals, and who did which task varied from place to place.

beats.scene: Hunters share the meat of a deer equally around a campfire
beats.summary: Studies of modern foraging peoples such as the Hadza suggest that early bands shared food and kept leaders weak.

beats.scene: An elder shows children how to track animal prints in the dust
beats.summary: Foragers knew an enormous amount about plants and animals, and passed it on by showing, telling and singing.

beats.scene: Two people talk and point toward the horizon beside a campfire
beats.summary: Nobody knows when language began, but speech let people warn, teach, plan and describe things that were not in front of them.

beats.scene: A woman threads shell beads while red ochre lies beside her in a cave
beats.summary: In Blombos Cave in South Africa, people at least 75,000 years ago made shell beads and scratched patterns on ochre.

beats.scene: A person sews animal skins with a bone needle near the fire
beats.summary: Bone needles from at least 40,000 years ago show that people sewed clothes, which helped them live in cold lands.

beats.scene: Painted animals and red handprints glow on a cave wall in torchlight
beats.summary: At least 40,000 years ago people were painting animals on cave walls, and the oldest known animal painting is in Indonesia.

beats.scene: A musician plays a flute made from a bird bone in a cave
beats.summary: Flutes made from bird bone and ivory about 40,000 years old have been found in Germany, and a small carved lion-man statue was found nearby.

beats.scene: Mourners lay a person in a grave covered with ivory beads and red powder
beats.summary: Some graves hold ornaments, showing that people marked death with care and perhaps belief, though we cannot know what they thought.

beats.scene: A jawbone and stone tools lie in the dust of a sea-view cave
beats.summary: Some Homo sapiens left Africa long before the main migration: a jawbone from Misliya Cave in Israel is about 180,000 years old.

beats.scene: Travellers walk in a line along a coast beside a wide blue sea
beats.summary: The main spread of our species across the world seems to have begun about 60,000 to 70,000 years ago.

beats.scene: Smoke and ash rise from a giant volcano above a dark tropical island
beats.summary: A giant volcano erupted at Toba in Sumatra about 74,000 years ago, but scientists disagree about how much it affected people.

beats.scene: Families gather shellfish and fish along a rocky shore under the morning sun
beats.summary: Coastlines gave rich food, and groups may have followed the shores of Arabia and southern Asia, moving slowly over many generations.

beats.scene: Modern people and Neanderthals face each other across a stream in a green valley
beats.summary: In Europe and Asia our ancestors met the Neanderthals and Denisovans, and the groups lived side by side for thousands of years.

beats.scene: A modern and an ancient face side by side, with a thread linking them
beats.summary: Our ancestors sometimes had children with Neanderthals and Denisovans, so a little of their DNA lives on in many people today.

beats.scene: Thin mountain air and climbers on a high snowy plateau in Tibet
beats.summary: Many Tibetans carry a gene from the Denisovans that helps the body cope with the thin air of high mountains.

beats.scene: A girl's bones rest in a cave beside a Neanderthal tool
beats.summary: Scientists found a girl, nicknamed Denny, whose mother was a Neanderthal and whose father was a Denisovan.

beats.scene: A last Neanderthal stands alone at the entrance of a cave at dusk
beats.summary: The Neanderthals died out about 40,000 years ago, and the other human species also vanished; scientists do not agree on why.

beats.scene: People on a simple raft paddle across open sea towards a distant shore
beats.summary: People reached Australia at least 50,000 years ago, which required crossing open sea in boats or rafts.

beats.scene: Walls of ice and snow stretch over a wide, windswept plain
beats.summary: About 26,000 to 20,000 years ago the last Ice Age was at its coldest, and huge sheets of ice covered northern lands.

beats.scene: People live in a house made of mammoth bones under a grey sky
beats.summary: Ice Age hunters in eastern Europe built houses from mammoth bones and hides, and wore sewn clothing against the cold.

beats.scene: A small carved figure of a woman rests in a hand beside a fire
beats.summary: Ice Age people carved small figures, such as the Venus of Willendorf, about 30,000 years old.

beats.scene: Painted horses and bison gallop across the walls of a deep cave
beats.summary: In the Lascaux cave in France, people painted more than a thousand animals about 17,000 years ago, using lamps and pigments.

beats.scene: A wolf cub sleeps near a fire while a hunter watches
beats.summary: Dogs, descended from wolves, were the first animals people tamed, at least 15,000 years ago and perhaps much earlier.

beats.scene: A group of people shelter in a windy treeless grassland between two glaciers
beats.summary: When the sea level was lower, a wide land called Beringia joined Siberia to Alaska, and people lived there for thousands of years.

beats.scene: Hunters in furs walk across a snowy land between two vast icy seas
beats.summary: During the last Ice Age, lower seas opened a route between Siberia and Alaska, and people reached the Americas at least 15,000 years ago.

beats.scene: Footprints in muddy ground beside a shallow lake in a desert valley
beats.summary: Human footprints in New Mexico may be about 21,000 to 23,000 years old, and some scientists think people arrived even earlier than 15,000 years ago.

beats.scene: A huge woolly mammoth stands in snow while small hunters watch from far away
beats.summary: As people spread, many giant animals died out, and scientists think hunting and a changing climate both played a part.

beats.scene: A hunter hurls a spear with a wooden launcher beside a fish stream
beats.summary: New tools such as spear-throwers, bows, nets and fish hooks made food easier to catch.

beats.scene: Green plants and wild grasses cover a warm valley beside a river
beats.summary: About 11,700 years ago the last Ice Age ended, and the warmer, steadier climate gave people new chances to find and grow food.

beats.scene: Rising sea water floods a grassy plain while people watch from higher ground
beats.summary: As the ice melted, the sea rose by about a hundred metres, drowning coastal plains and turning Britain into an island.

beats.scene: Women harvest wild grain with stone blades beside round stone houses
beats.summary: In the Middle East, wild food was so rich that people called the Natufians settled in villages about 14,000 years ago, long before farming.

beats.scene: A woman kneads dough beside a stone hearth while another stirs grain
beats.summary: Charred crumbs found in Jordan show that people baked flat bread about 14,400 years ago, and traces in a cave in Israel suggest early brewing.

beats.scene: Huge carved stone pillars stand in a circle on a hilltop
beats.summary: At Göbekli Tepe in Turkey, hunter-gatherers raised circles of carved stone pillars about 11,500 years ago, before farming began.

beats.scene: A stone tower and thick wall rise above mud houses beside a spring
beats.summary: At Jericho, a small town by a spring, people built a stone tower and wall about 10,000 years ago.

beats.scene: Farmers scatter seed and cut ripe wheat in a sunny field
beats.summary: About 11,000 years ago people in the Fertile Crescent began to plant crops; farming began independently in several other places too.

beats.scene: A map with five glowing patches showing places where farming began
beats.summary: Farming began separately in China, Mexico, New Guinea, the Andes and Africa, using rice, maize, taro, potatoes and sorghum.

beats.scene: A farmer plants seeds beside a patch of wild grass in the morning light
beats.summary: There was no single cause of farming; it grew slowly, over thousands of years, as people tended wild plants more and more.

beats.scene: A farmer leads a sheep and a goat past a small mud house
beats.summary: People tamed sheep, goats, cattle and pigs, and learned to use them for meat, milk and wool; dogs had joined people earlier.

beats.scene: A tired farmer bends over a field while a hunter rests nearby
beats.summary: Farming fed more people per field, but early farmers often worked harder, ate less varied food and caught diseases from animals.

beats.scene: A sick child lies in a crowded mud house, animals in the yard
beats.summary: Living close together and near animals let diseases spread, and many illnesses, such as flu, came to people from animals.

beats.scene: A herder drinks fresh milk beside a flock of cattle on open grassland
beats.summary: Among herding peoples, a gene that lets adults digest milk spread widely, a case of our bodies changing along with our way of life.

beats.scene: A potter shapes a clay jar on a wheel beside a baking kiln
beats.summary: Clay pots let people store grain and cook in new ways, and the first pots were made in East Asia by hunter-gatherers about 20,000 years ago.

beats.scene: Flat-roofed mud houses packed together with people climbing ladders on the roofs
beats.summary: Some villages grew into towns; Çatalhöyük in Turkey, about 9,000 years ago, had houses so close together that people walked on the roofs.

beats.scene: Workers pour grain into a large storehouse while a ruler watches
beats.summary: Stored grain was a kind of wealth; those who controlled it often became rulers, and inequality grew.

beats.scene: A rich grave with gold ornaments beside simple graves with few objects
beats.summary: In a graveyard at Varna in Bulgaria, about 6,500 years ago, a few people were buried with gold ornaments, which shows that some had become far richer than others.

beats.scene: A farmer builds a fence around his land while neighbours look on
beats.summary: Land became valuable, and with it came fences, quarrels and sometimes violence, though scientists disagree about how common war was.

beats.scene: A smith heats green stones in a hot clay furnace beside a mountain
beats.summary: About 7,000 years ago people in Europe and Asia learned to melt copper out of rock, and the Iceman of the Alps carried a copper axe 5,300 years ago.

beats.scene: Huge standing stones in a circle at sunrise on an open grassy plain
beats.summary: As farming spread to Europe, farmers raised great monuments, such as Stonehenge in Britain, about 5,000 years ago, without any writing.

beats.scene: Canals carry river water to green fields on a flat dry plain
beats.summary: In Mesopotamia, the land between the Tigris and Euphrates, farmers dug canals to bring river water to their fields, and the first cities grew there.

beats.scene: A walled city of mud brick with a tall temple rising above flat roofs
beats.summary: Uruk, in Mesopotamia, was one of the world's first cities, with tens of thousands of people about 5,000 years ago.

beats.scene: A scribe presses marks into a soft clay tablet with a reed
beats.summary: Writing began about 5,300 years ago in Mesopotamia, first for keeping accounts of grain, beer and cloth.

beats.scene: Students sit on benches copying wedge-shaped signs onto clay tablets
beats.summary: Cuneiform, the wedge-shaped writing of Mesopotamia, was used for about 3,000 years, and trained scribes learned it in school.

beats.scene: A papyrus scroll covered in colourful hieroglyphs lies beside a pen and ink
beats.summary: Writing was invented again in Egypt, China and Mexico, and Egyptians wrote on papyrus, a paper made from river reeds.

beats.scene: A priestess in a long robe reads a poem by lamplight in a temple
beats.summary: Enheduanna, a priestess and poet who lived about 4,300 years ago, is the first author in history we know by name.

beats.scene: A king and a wild man wrestle in a city street beneath tall walls
beats.summary: The Epic of Gilgamesh, a story about a king of Uruk, is one of the oldest great stories, written down about 4,000 years ago.

beats.scene: A tall carved stone stands in a crowded city square
beats.summary: Large cities needed shared rules; about 3,700 years ago King Hammurabi of Babylon had nearly 300 laws carved on a stone for all to see.

beats.scene: A great stone pyramid rises beside a river with workers and boats
beats.summary: In Egypt, beside the Nile, the Great Pyramid of Giza was built about 4,500 years ago as a royal tomb, showing how many people a ruler could organise.

beats.scene: Straight streets, brick houses and drains in a planned city beside a river
beats.summary: The cities of the Indus Valley, about 4,500 years ago, had planned streets, drains and standard weights, but their writing has not been read.

beats.scene: A wooden cart with solid wheels rolls along a dusty track
beats.summary: The wheel appeared about 5,500 years ago, first for pottery and then for carts, which made it easier to carry heavy loads.

beats.scene: A rider gallops across open grassland while a light chariot races beside him
beats.summary: On the grasslands of Eurasia, people learned to ride horses and, about 4,000 years ago, built light chariots with spoked wheels.

beats.scene: A wooden boat with a square sail crosses a calm river
beats.summary: Boats with sails on the Nile and the seas carried goods more cheaply than any cart could.

beats.scene: A smith pours glowing bronze into a mould beside a hot furnace
beats.summary: People learned to mix copper and tin to make bronze about 5,000 years ago, and bronze tools and weapons were harder than copper.

beats.scene: A burning city wall and a few boats leave a harbour at dusk
beats.summary: Around 3,200 years ago, many Bronze Age cities in the eastern Mediterranean fell, perhaps because of drought, earthquakes, raiders and failing trade.

beats.scene: A blacksmith hammers a glowing iron blade on an anvil
beats.summary: Iron came into wide use about 3,000 years ago; it was cheaper than bronze, because iron ore is found almost everywhere.

beats.scene: Sailors unload jars and cloth from a trading ship in a busy harbour
beats.summary: About 3,000 years ago Phoenician sailors traded across the Mediterranean and spread a simple alphabet of 22 letters.

beats.scene: A merchant weighs silver on a scale while a customer holds out a cloth
beats.summary: Before coins, people traded by swapping goods or by weighing silver, which was slow and needed trust.

beats.scene: A trader presses a stamped gold coin into a customer's hand
beats.summary: The first coins we know of were made in Lydia, in modern Turkey, about 2,600 years ago, and each had a stamp to show its weight and value.

beats.scene: A merchant counts paper money beside a stack of copper coins in a market
beats.summary: About 1,000 years ago China began to print paper money, which works only because people trust it.

beats.scene: A king on a throne receives gifts from many kneeling visitors in different dress
beats.summary: An empire is a state that rules many peoples; the first known was founded by Sargon of Akkad about 4,300 years ago.

beats.scene: A long road with riders and messengers crossing a wide sandy landscape
beats.summary: Large empires such as Persia, Rome and Qin China used roads, messengers and armies to rule huge areas.

beats.scene: A young general on horseback leads soldiers across a mountain pass towards a river
beats.summary: Alexander the Great, a Macedonian king, conquered lands from Greece to India and died young, in 323 BCE, about 2,300 years ago.

beats.scene: A king reads carved stone pillars at the edge of a quiet battlefield
beats.summary: Ashoka, who ruled much of India about 2,300 years ago, turned away from war after a terrible battle and carved messages of kindness on pillars.

beats.scene: Rows of clay soldiers stand in a huge underground hall
beats.summary: In 221 BCE China was united under the First Emperor, who standardised writing, money and measures and was buried with an army of clay soldiers.

beats.scene: A paper maker spreads pulp on a screen beside a river in China
beats.summary: Under the Han dynasty, China's rulers kept a large army and fine roads, and paper had been invented by about 2,000 years ago.

beats.scene: A Roman road runs straight across hills beside a high stone bridge
beats.summary: Rome grew from one city into an empire around the Mediterranean, and built about 80,000 kilometres of good roads.

beats.scene: A stone aqueduct carries water across a valley beside a crowded Roman town
beats.summary: Romans built aqueducts, public baths and concrete buildings, and spread Latin, which became the mother of Spanish, French and Italian.

beats.scene: Gladiators in an arena and chained workers in a field
beats.summary: Roman wealth rested on slavery; millions of people were enslaved, and in 73 BCE Spartacus led a famous slave revolt.

beats.scene: Tall carved stone pillars in a city rising above a green jungle
beats.summary: Great states also grew outside Eurasia: the Maya built stone cities in Mexico and Central America, and Aksum in Africa traded with Rome and India.

beats.scene: Three thinkers in different robes sit under trees, speaking to students
beats.summary: Around 2,500 years ago, thinkers such as Confucius, the Buddha and Socrates asked how people should live, and many beliefs spread widely afterwards.

beats.scene: A teacher in plain robes talks to students in a courtyard in ancient China
beats.summary: Confucius taught that people should learn, respect others and rule with fairness, and his sayings were collected by his followers.

beats.scene: A prince in fine clothes sits under a tree beside poor travellers
beats.summary: The Buddha, born as a prince in northern India, taught a path of understanding and compassion, and Buddhism spread across Asia.

beats.scene: Citizens raise hands to vote in a stone open-air meeting place in Athens
beats.summary: In Athens, about 2,500 years ago, citizens met to decide laws themselves, although women, enslaved people and foreigners could not take part.

beats.scene: A priest reads aloud from a scroll to a gathered crowd
beats.summary: Several faiths grew from ancient roots; the Hebrew Bible records the belief in one God, and Hindu hymns, the Vedas, were first spoken aloud over 3,000 years ago.

beats.scene: Travellers listen to a speaker under an olive tree in the Roman world
beats.summary: Christianity began about 2,000 years ago in the Roman Empire from the teachings of Jesus, and grew to be one of the largest religions.

beats.scene: Pilgrims in a desert city face a square black building at sunrise
beats.summary: Islam began in Arabia about 1,400 years ago with the teaching of Muhammad, and spread quickly from Spain to the edge of India.

beats.scene: A traveller carries a book, a bowl and a staff along a mountain road
beats.summary: Faiths travelled along trade routes; they gave people shared stories, rules and charity, though they have also divided them.

beats.scene: A caravan of camels carries bundles of silk along a desert road
beats.summary: From about 2,100 years ago, roads and sea routes linked China with the Mediterranean, carrying silk, spices, ideas and diseases.

beats.scene: Wooden ships with triangular sails cross a blue sea beside a distant coast
beats.summary: Traders used the monsoon winds to sail across the Indian Ocean, linking Arabia, India, East Africa and China.

beats.scene: Scholars read and copy books in a bright library with tall shelves
beats.summary: In Baghdad, about 1,200 years ago, scholars gathered in a House of Wisdom and translated Greek, Persian and Indian books into Arabic.

beats.scene: A teacher draws a circle in the sand while students write numbers on slates
beats.summary: Mathematicians in India treated zero as a number, and scholars such as al-Khwarizmi spread the idea; his work gave us the words algebra and algorithm.

beats.scene: A scholar in a dark room watches a beam of light through a hole
beats.summary: Ibn al-Haytham, about 1,000 years ago, tested how light and sight work by experiment, and Ibn Sina's medical encyclopaedia was used for centuries.

beats.scene: Workers press paper onto carved wooden blocks and a fire flashes in a pot
beats.summary: Chinese inventors made paper, printed books, gunpowder and the magnetic compass long before they reached Europe.

beats.scene: A king in golden robes rides at the head of a long desert caravan
beats.summary: Mansa Musa, the king of Mali, made a famous pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324 with so much gold that prices rose in Cairo, and Timbuktu became a city of scholars.

beats.scene: Stone roads climb steep mountains to a city; a messenger holds knotted cords
beats.summary: The Inca in the Andes ruled by roads, runners and knotted cords called quipu, while the Aztec built a great city on an island in a lake.

beats.scene: Wooden canoes with sails cross a huge ocean under the stars
beats.summary: Polynesian sailors crossed the vast Pacific by reading stars, waves and birds, and reached Hawaii, Easter Island and New Zealand.

beats.scene: A longship with a dragon head lands on a cold northern beach
beats.summary: The Vikings of Scandinavia raided and traded across Europe, and sailed to Iceland, Greenland and North America about 1,000 years ago.

beats.scene: A castle, a church tower and monks reading in a quiet stone cloister
beats.summary: In medieval Europe most people were farmers, monasteries kept learning alive, and the first universities began in the 1100s.

beats.scene: Mongol horsemen gallop across a wide grass plain towards a walled city
beats.summary: In the 1200s the Mongols created the largest land empire in history, destroying cities but also opening trade routes.

beats.scene: Rats and fleas crowd the deck of a trading ship entering a harbour
beats.summary: The Black Death was caused by a germ carried by fleas on rats, and it travelled along the trade routes from Asia to Europe in 1347.

beats.scene: A quiet empty street in a medieval town with closed doors
beats.summary: The Black Death of 1347 to 1351 spread along trade routes and may have killed a third or more of the people in Europe.

beats.scene: Workers in a field bargain with a landowner over wages in a village
beats.summary: With so many workers dead, those who survived could ask for higher pay, and in western Europe many peasants gained more freedom.

beats.scene: Guards stop a ship at a harbour while sailors wait on deck
beats.summary: People did not know about germs, but port cities began to keep ships and travellers waiting for thirty and later forty days, which gave us the word quarantine.

beats.scene: A painter at an easel in a bright Italian workshop paints a lifelike scene
beats.summary: In the Italian cities of the 1400s, rich merchants paid artists and scholars, and the Renaissance began, a rebirth of interest in art and old learning.

beats.scene: A huge Chinese treasure ship with nine masts sails beside small boats
beats.summary: Between 1405 and 1433, the Chinese admiral Zheng He led huge fleets of treasure ships to India, Arabia and East Africa.

beats.scene: A printer pulls the lever of a wooden press beside a pile of pages
beats.summary: Around 1450, Gutenberg's press with movable metal type made books cheaper and ideas faster to spread.

beats.scene: Rows of metal letters lie in a tray beside a small ink-stained press
beats.summary: Printing with movable type was not invented once, for Korea and China had it earlier, but the alphabet suited it and the press spread fast in Europe.

beats.scene: A crowd reads a printed sheet pinned to a church door
beats.summary: By 1500, about 20 million printed books existed in Europe, and printing helped Martin Luther's ideas spread in the 1500s.

beats.scene: Cannons fire at the thick stone walls of a great city by the sea
beats.summary: In 1453 Ottoman cannons broke the walls of Constantinople, and gunpowder weapons changed how wars were fought.

beats.scene: A small three-masted ship with a compass on deck sails along a coast
beats.summary: In the 1400s Portuguese sailors explored the coast of Africa with new ships, compasses and maps, hoping to reach the riches of Asia by sea.

beats.scene: Wooden ships reach a busy tropical port with palm trees and spice stalls
beats.summary: In 1498 Vasco da Gama sailed around Africa to India, opening a sea route that let Europeans trade directly with Asia.

beats.scene: A wooden sailing ship with three masts crosses wide waves under a bright sun
beats.summary: In 1492 Columbus crossed the Atlantic and reached the Americas, beginning lasting contact between the hemispheres; ships soon sailed around the world.

beats.scene: A battered ship returns to a Spanish harbour with a few weary sailors
beats.summary: From 1519 to 1522 a Spanish fleet sailed right around the world; Magellan died on the way, and only one ship and about 18 men returned.

beats.scene: Crops, animals and ships crossing between two continents on a map
beats.summary: After 1492, crops, animals and diseases crossed the ocean in both directions; diseases killed huge numbers of people in the Americas.

beats.scene: A basket of potatoes, maize, tomatoes and chillies beside a field of wheat
beats.summary: Potatoes, maize, tomatoes and chocolate went from the Americas to the rest of the world, while horses, wheat, cattle and sugar went the other way.

beats.scene: Soldiers and local allies march towards a great lake city under tall volcanoes
beats.summary: In 1521 Spanish soldiers, with thousands of local allies and the help of smallpox, overthrew the Aztec empire, and the Inca fell about ten years later.

beats.scene: Miners carry baskets of rock out of a steep silver mountain
beats.summary: From the 1540s, silver from mines such as Potosí in Bolivia flowed to Europe and China, linking the world's economies for the first time.

beats.scene: A large ship at a harbour with people in chains waiting on the quay
beats.summary: From the 1500s to the 1800s, more than 10 million people were taken from Africa and forced to work as slaves in the Americas.

beats.scene: Merchants buy and sell paper shares at tables in a busy Dutch trading hall
beats.summary: In 1602 the Dutch East India Company sold shares to the public, and companies became powerful players in global trade.

beats.scene: A scholar draws circles of planets around a bright sun beside an open book
beats.summary: In 1543 Copernicus published the idea that the Earth moves around the Sun, which challenged centuries of belief.

beats.scene: A man looks through a long brass telescope at the night sky
beats.summary: From the 1500s a new way of finding out spread, based on observation and experiment; Galileo's telescope in 1610 showed moons around Jupiter.

beats.scene: An old man stands before stern judges in robes in a grand hall
beats.summary: In 1633 Galileo was forced by a Church court to say that the Earth does not move, and he spent his last years under house arrest.

beats.scene: A man peers into a small brass microscope at a drop of water
beats.summary: Early microscopes showed a hidden world: Hooke named the cell in 1665, and Leeuwenhoek saw tiny living things in pond water.

beats.scene: A man sits under an apple tree while the Moon rises above the hills
beats.summary: In 1687 Isaac Newton showed that one law of gravity explains why an apple falls and why the Moon circles the Earth.

beats.scene: Scientists in wigs examine a glass vessel at a table in a meeting room
beats.summary: Scientists began to share, test and correct each other's work in societies and journals, and science grew by admitting mistakes.

beats.scene: People gather to read pamphlets and debate in a coffee house
beats.summary: In the 1700s writers in Europe argued for reason, free speech and rights, and the American and French revolutions followed in 1776 and 1789.

beats.scene: Men and women hold a banner and a petition beside a harbour
beats.summary: In the late 1700s a movement to end the slave trade grew, and Britain banned it in 1807 and ended slavery in its empire in 1833.

beats.scene: A young man studies finches and plants on a rocky island shore
beats.summary: Charles Darwin's 1859 book explained evolution by natural selection, showing that all living things, including humans, share common ancestors.

beats.scene: A woman paints a caterpillar and a leaf while another reads beside a telescope
beats.summary: Women often were shut out of universities but contributed to science, as Maria Merian studied insects and Émilie du Châtelet explained Newton.

beats.scene: A steam engine drives machines in a large smoky factory hall
beats.summary: From about 1760, Britain began to use coal, steam engines and factories on a large scale, and many people moved to cities.

beats.scene: Miners carry coal from a deep pit to a puffing steam engine above
beats.summary: Coal is stored energy from ancient plants, and steam engines let people do work that once needed the muscles of many people and animals.

beats.scene: Tall chimneys and crowded brick houses stretch across a smoky city skyline
beats.summary: Cities grew at astonishing speed; by about 1800 London had passed one million people, and many city streets were crowded and dirty.

beats.scene: Children in ragged clothes work at noisy machines in a cotton mill
beats.summary: Factory work was long and hard, and children worked in mills and mines until laws and unions slowly improved conditions.

beats.scene: A steam train crosses a hill while passengers wave from the windows
beats.summary: In the 1800s railways made travel much faster, and the first passenger railway opened in England in 1825.

beats.scene: A man taps a telegraph key while a long wire stretches into the distance
beats.summary: The telegraph, first used for messages in 1844, sent news along wires in moments, and a lasting cable crossed the Atlantic in 1866.

beats.scene: An early electric light bulb glows in a dark room beside a large generator
beats.summary: Electricity changed homes and factories; electric lamps became practical in the 1870s, and power stations and telephones followed.

beats.scene: A black motor car with a crank handle stands beside a country road
beats.summary: Karl Benz built a petrol car in 1885, and Henry Ford's assembly line made cars cheap enough for ordinary families by the 1910s.

beats.scene: A graph line curving steeply upwards beside crowds of people
beats.summary: The human population passed one billion about 1800, and reached eight billion in 2022.

beats.scene: A European ship unloads goods in a colonial port beside local workers
beats.summary: By 1914 European states ruled much of Africa and Asia, usually without asking the people who lived there, and many peoples resisted.

beats.scene: A mother holds a healthy baby while a doctor checks a wall chart
beats.summary: For most of history many children died young; in about 1800 more than four in ten died before the age of five, and today it is about four in a hundred.

beats.scene: A doctor gives an injection to a child while a nurse looks on
beats.summary: In 1796 Edward Jenner showed that a mild illness, cowpox, could protect people from smallpox, and the word vaccine comes from the Latin for cow.

beats.scene: Health workers hold up a poster in a crowded village while villagers queue
beats.summary: Smallpox, which killed hundreds of millions of people, was wiped out by 1980 after a worldwide campaign of vaccination.

beats.scene: A doctor in a long coat washes his hands beside a hospital bed
beats.summary: In the 1800s doctors such as Semmelweis, Snow, Pasteur and Koch showed that tiny germs cause many diseases, and that washing hands and clean water save lives.

beats.scene: Workers lay a huge brick sewer tunnel under a busy city street
beats.summary: Clean water and sewers did more to save lives than almost any medicine, and London built a great sewer system in the 1860s.

beats.scene: A scientist examines a glass dish where mould has killed bacteria
beats.summary: In 1928 Alexander Fleming noticed that a mould killed bacteria, which led to penicillin and the antibiotics that now cure many infections.

beats.scene: A farmer spreads fertiliser on a green field of tall wheat
beats.summary: In the early 1900s two German chemists, Haber and Bosch, found how to make fertiliser from the air; many experts think about half of us now eat food grown with it.

beats.scene: A scientist in a field holds a short, sturdy ear of wheat
beats.summary: In the 1960s Norman Borlaug and other scientists bred short, strong wheat that gave far bigger harvests in Mexico, India and Pakistan.

beats.scene: Rows of small houses with lights and a school and market
beats.summary: In 1820 about eight in ten people lived in extreme poverty, but today the share is under one in ten, though many millions are still poor.

beats.scene: A mother and father with a small family beside a school and clinic
beats.summary: As more children survived and women gained education and rights, families grew smaller, and the growth of the world's population began to slow.

beats.scene: Soldiers in muddy trenches look across a bare, broken field
beats.summary: The First World War of 1914 to 1918 used machine guns and factory-made weapons, and killed about ten million soldiers and millions of civilians.

beats.scene: People wearing cloth masks queue outside a crowded hospital tent
beats.summary: A flu pandemic in 1918 and 1919 spread around the world on ships and trains and killed an estimated 50 million people.

beats.scene: A destroyed street at dusk with a lone figure and a distant glow
beats.summary: The Second World War of 1939 to 1945 killed tens of millions of people, including six million Jews murdered by Nazi Germany in the Holocaust.

beats.scene: A tall pale cloud rises over a flattened city beside a river
beats.summary: In 1945 the first atomic bombs were used on Japan, and after the war nuclear weapons became so dangerous that none has been used in war since.

beats.scene: Delegates from many countries sit in a great round hall beneath a blue flag
beats.summary: In 1945 the United Nations was founded, human rights were set out in 1948, and many colonies became independent countries.

beats.scene: A small propeller aeroplane lifts off a windy beach
beats.summary: In 1903 the Wright brothers made the first powered flight, which lasted twelve seconds, and within a lifetime jet planes carried millions of people.

beats.scene: A rocket stands on a launch pad as flames and smoke begin to rise
beats.summary: In 1957 the first satellite, Sputnik, orbited the Earth, and in 1961 Yuri Gagarin became the first person in space.

beats.scene: An astronaut in a white suit stands on the grey Moon beside a flag
beats.summary: In 1969, only 66 years after the first flight, Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin walked on the Moon.

beats.scene: A small blue and white Earth rises over a grey Moon horizon
beats.summary: In 1968 astronauts photographed the Earth rising over the Moon, and the picture of our small, fragile planet inspired many people to protect it.

beats.scene: A person holds a glowing phone beside a very old room-sized computer
beats.summary: Computers, once as big as rooms, became tiny and powerful; the web began about 1990, and more than five billion people now use the internet.

beats.scene: Smoking chimneys and a busy road under a hazy evening sky
beats.summary: Burning coal, oil and gas adds carbon dioxide to the air, and the planet has warmed by a little more than one degree Celsius.

beats.scene: A melting glacier, a cracked dry riverbed and a flooded street side by side
beats.summary: Warming brings stronger heat waves, droughts and floods and raises the sea, and in 2015 nearly every country agreed in Paris to limit it.

beats.scene: A wild animal watches from a forest edge beside fields of cattle
beats.summary: Humans and their farm animals now make up most of the weight of all mammals, and many wild species are in danger as their homes shrink.

beats.scene: A lone pigeon sits on a branch in an empty, silent forest
beats.summary: The last passenger pigeon died in 1914, and scientists warn that up to a million species of plants and animals may be at risk of dying out.

beats.scene: A whale rises through bright waters beside a calm blue sea
beats.summary: People can solve shared problems: a world treaty stopped the chemicals that harmed the ozone layer, and whale hunting was largely banned in 1986.

beats.scene: Rows of solar panels and tall wind turbines stand across green hills
beats.summary: Clean energy from the sun and wind has become much cheaper, and many countries are building more of it each year.

beats.scene: A scientist looks at a long strip of coloured code on a bright screen
beats.summary: In 2003 scientists finished reading the full human genome, and it confirmed that any two people are almost exactly the same in their DNA.

beats.scene: A student and a robot study a glowing screen in a classroom
beats.summary: New tools, such as gene editing and artificial intelligence, give people great power, and societies must decide how to use them wisely.

beats.scene: A line of scenes from a campfire to a city skyline and a satellite
beats.summary: Humans took over the world by sharing what they know: language, writing, trade, science and the internet let each generation build on the last.

beats.scene: People of many ages and skin colours stand together looking at the sunrise
beats.summary: All people alive today are one species with almost identical DNA; the story is unfinished, and the choices we make now will shape the next chapter.

Fewer people are very poor now than in 1820, but many still are.
When more children lived, families had fewer babies, and growth slowed down.
The First World War began in 1914, and millions of soldiers died.
In 1918, a flu spread around the world and killed millions of people.
The Second World War killed tens of millions of people, and was terrible.
In 1945, atomic bombs were used on Japan, and no country has used them since.
After the war, many countries joined the United Nations to keep the peace.
In 1903, the Wright brothers flew a plane for twelve seconds.
In 1961, Yuri Gagarin became the first person to travel in space.
In 1969, Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin walked on the Moon.
Pictures of the Earth from space made many people want to protect it.
Computers became small, and now most people can use the internet.
Burning coal and oil adds gas to the air, and the world is warming.
A warmer world brings more floods, droughts and hot days.
People and farm animals are now most of the weight of all mammals.
Many kinds of wild animals are in danger, and some have already gone.
People can solve big problems, and the whale is one good example.
The sun and wind can give clean power, and it is now cheaper.
Scientists read all of human DNA, and everyone is almost the same.
We have new tools, and we must decide how to use them well.
We took over the world because we shared what we learned.
All humans share one story, and we can choose what happens next.
B1B2: Humans are only one of millions of kinds of animal on Earth. Yet no other animal has built cities, crossed oceans or left footprints on the Moon.

Our planet is about four and a half billion years old, and life has been on it for most of that time. If the whole story of Earth were squeezed into one day, our species would arrive only in the last few seconds before midnight.
About 66 million years ago a huge rock from space hit the Earth, and the big dinosaurs died out. Small furry mammals, which had lived in their shadow, then had room to spread and change.
Primates, the group that includes monkeys, apes and humans, have hands that can grip and eyes that look forward. Most of them live in groups, and they learn a great deal from one another.
Humans are not separate from the animal world, because we are one of the great apes, like gorillas and orangutans. Our closest living relatives are the chimpanzees and the bonobos.

Scientists think that humans and chimpanzees share an ancestor that lived in Africa about six to seven million years ago. Over time its descendants slowly divided into two lines, and one of them eventually led to us.

At Laetoli in Tanzania, early human relatives left a line of footprints in soft volcanic ash more than three and a half million years ago. The ash hardened like cement, and the prints show that they walked upright on two legs.
Scientists still argue about why our ancestors began to walk upright, but the change was a big one. It freed their hands to carry food and babies, and it may also have saved energy.

In 1974 scientists in Ethiopia found about forty per cent of the skeleton of a small adult who lived roughly three million years ago. They named her Lucy, and she walked upright although her brain was no bigger than a chimpanzee's.

By about two and a half million years ago, our relatives in Africa were breaking stones to make sharp flakes. These simple tools could cut meat from bones and crack them open to reach the rich food inside.

Between two and three million years ago, a new group of early humans appeared in Africa, and scientists call it Homo. One of its first members, Homo habilis, had a larger brain than Lucy's and made stone tools.

Nearly two million years ago a taller kind of human called Homo erectus appeared in Africa. Its long legs were made for walking, and a famous skeleton of a boy found in Kenya shows a body very much like ours.

Homo erectus made hand axes by chipping both sides of a stone until it had a sharp, teardrop-shaped edge. The same design was used for over a million years, which suggests that skills were passed on from one generation to the next.

Homo erectus was the first human to leave Africa, and bones about 1,800,000 years old have been found in Georgia. Later groups spread across Asia, and their remains have been discovered in places as far apart as Java and China.

At some point our ancestors learned to control fire, which gave them warmth, light and protection. Scientists disagree about when, but ash and burnt bones in a South African cave are about a million years old.

Fire kept dangerous animals away from the sleeping camp, and it turned the dark hours into time for talking and working. People also learned that holding the point of a wooden spear in the flames made it harder and sharper.

Cooking made food softer and easier to digest, so the body needed less energy to break it down. Some scientists believe this helped to feed the human brain, which uses far more energy than any other part of the body.

Over about two million years the human brain grew to roughly three times the size of Lucy's. Human babies were born helpless, so they needed years of care, and groups that shared the work of feeding and protecting children did better.

In a marsh at Schöningen in Germany, hunters about 300,000 years ago made beautiful wooden spears from spruce trees. The spears were balanced like javelins, and the bones of butchered horses nearby suggest that the hunters worked together.

By about 300,000 years ago, descendants of earlier humans lived in Africa, Europe and Asia, and they were slowly becoming different from each other. DNA shows that the ancestors of the Neanderthals and of our own species had separated some time between 500,000 and 700,000 years ago.

The oldest bones that look like ours were found at Jebel Irhoud in Morocco, and they are about 300,000 years old. The faces of these people were very like ours, but their skulls were still longer and lower.

Other very old bones from Ethiopia and South Africa show that Homo sapiens grew up in many parts of the continent. Groups probably met and married across large distances, so our species did not begin in one single place.

Neanderthals were strong, stocky people with wide noses and powerful arms, and they lived in Europe and western Asia for more than 300,000 years. Their brains were as large as ours, and they hunted big animals such as deer, horses and even mammoths.

Neanderthals made fire, wooden spears and stone tools, and they even made glue from birch tree tar to fix tools together. Bones from a cave in Iraq show that they cared for sick and injured people, who sometimes lived for years afterwards.

A few finds in Spain and elsewhere suggest that Neanderthals painted red marks and wore shell ornaments. Many scientists believe this is true, but others think the dates may be wrong, so the argument continues.

In 2010 scientists took DNA from a finger bone found in Denisova Cave in Siberia, and it did not match Neanderthals or us. It showed that a different group, now called the Denisovans, had lived in Asia, although we know them mostly from a few bones and teeth.

On the island of Flores in Indonesia, scientists found the bones of adults who were only a little over a metre tall. They are known as Homo floresiensis, or the hobbit, and they may have lived there until about 50,000 years ago.

In a deep cave system in South Africa, scientists found the bones of a small-brained human called Homo naledi. It lived about 300,000 years ago, at the same time as the first Homo sapiens, which came as a surprise to many experts.

At a place in Kenya, people about 300,000 years ago carried black volcanic glass and red pigments over many miles. This shows that groups traded or at least met one another, which would have helped them to share ideas and to survive hard times.

For most of its history our species shared the world with other kinds of human, including Neanderthals, Denisovans and small groups in Asia and Africa. Why we alone survived is one of the great questions of science, and nobody has found a single answer.

For almost all of human history, people lived in small bands of a few dozen, and they moved from place to place with the seasons. They followed the fruit, the fish and the herds, and they carried few possessions.

Foragers gathered fruit, nuts, roots and honey, and they hunted animals and caught fish. Who did which task varied from place to place, and both women and men probably knew a great deal about plants and animals.

Some scientists study modern foraging peoples, such as the Hadza of Tanzania, to understand how early bands may have lived. These groups share food widely and do not let one person become too powerful, but the past may have been different.

A band's survival depended on knowledge about where water could be found, which plants were safe and how animals behaved. Children learned all of this by watching, listening to stories and joining in songs, so that nothing important was forgotten.
Nobody knows when language began, because speech leaves no fossils. It let people warn of danger, teach skills and describe things that were not in front of them.

In Blombos Cave in South Africa, people at least 75,000 years ago made beads from tiny sea shells. They also scratched patterns onto pieces of red ochre, a sign that they already used symbols to show who they were.

Fine bone needles about 40,000 years old have been found in Siberia, which show that people were sewing clothes from animal skins. Warm clothing allowed our ancestors to survive in cold lands where no human had lived before.

At least 40,000 years ago people began painting animals and red handprints on cave walls by the light of torches. The oldest known painting of an animal, a wild pig, was found on the Indonesian island of Sulawesi, and it is about 45,000 years old.

In caves in Germany, archaeologists found flutes made from bird bone and ivory that are about 40,000 years old. Nearby was a small statue of a lion-headed human carved from mammoth ivory, which suggests that these people also had stories and shared beliefs.

Some ancient graves, such as those at Sunghir in Russia, hold thousands of ivory beads and other ornaments. Such burials show that people took great care of the dead, but we can only guess what they believed about death.

A few groups of Homo sapiens left Africa long before the main migration, as a jawbone from Misliya Cave in Israel shows. It is about 180,000 years old, but those early travellers seem to have died out or to have been absorbed by others.

The main spread of our species across the world seems to have begun about 60,000 to 70,000 years ago. The people who left Africa then were the ancestors of almost everyone who lives outside Africa today.

About 74,000 years ago a giant volcano erupted at Toba in Sumatra, and ash covered much of southern Asia. Scientists disagree about how much it harmed human groups, and some think the effect was small.

The shores of the sea offered shellfish, fish and seabirds, so food was easier to find there than inland. Groups may have followed the coasts of Arabia and southern Asia, moving only a few kilometres in each generation.

When our ancestors reached Europe and Asia, they met Neanderthals and Denisovans, and the groups lived side by side for thousands of years. We do not know how they treated each other, but we know that they sometimes met as friends or families.

Ancient DNA shows that our ancestors sometimes had children with Neanderthals and Denisovans. Because of this, many people today carry a little of their DNA, usually between one and two per cent in people from Europe or Asia.

Many Tibetans carry a gene that came from the Denisovans, and it helps the body to cope with the thin air of high mountains. This is a good example of how a gene from another group of humans can still be useful today.

In Denisova Cave, scientists found a small bone that belonged to a girl who died about 90,000 years ago. Her DNA showed that her mother was a Neanderthal and her father was a Denisovan, so she is known as Denny.

The Neanderthals died out about 40,000 years ago, and the other human species also vanished. Climate change, disease, small numbers of people and competition with our own species have all been suggested, but scientists do not agree.
People reached Australia at least 50,000 years ago, and some scientists think it was even earlier. To get there they had to cross open sea in boats or rafts, so they must have been skilled sailors.

About 26,000 to 20,000 years ago the last Ice Age was at its coldest, and thick sheets of ice covered much of North America and northern Europe. So much water was frozen that the sea was more than a hundred metres lower than it is today.

In eastern Europe, hunters built houses from mammoth bones and animal skins, and they heated them with small fires. They wore sewn clothes, and some of their camps were used for many years, because the herds returned each season.

Ice Age people carved small figures of women from stone, bone and ivory, and the Venus of Willendorf is about 30,000 years old. Nobody knows what these figures meant, and archaeologists have many different ideas about them.

In the cave of Lascaux in France, people painted more than a thousand horses, bulls and deer about 17,000 years ago. They ground coloured earth into powder and used small stone lamps, and the paintings still look fresh today.

Dogs are descended from wolves, and they were probably the first animals that people tamed. DNA suggests that dogs were living with people at least 15,000 years ago, and some scientists believe they began even earlier.
When the sea level was low, a wide land called Beringia joined Siberia to Alaska. It was cold and windy, but it had grass and animals, and people may have lived there for thousands of years.

During the last Ice Age, the low seas opened a route between Siberia and Alaska, and people moved into the Americas. Most scientists agree that they had arrived at least 15,000 years ago, but the exact date is still debated.

Human footprints in the mud beside an ancient lake in New Mexico are probably between 21,000 and 23,000 years old. If this is correct, people reached the Americas even earlier than most scientists had thought, but the dating is still discussed.

As people spread, many giant animals died out, including mammoths, giant sloths and huge kangaroos. Scientists think that hunting and a changing climate both played a part, and they still debate which was more important.

New tools made hunting and fishing easier, such as spear-throwers, which let a hunter throw a spear much farther. Bows, nets and fish hooks followed, and with them people could catch more food and feed larger groups.
About 11,700 years ago the last Ice Age ended, and the world became warmer and wetter. This new climate was steadier than before, which gave people better chances to find and grow food.
As the great ice sheets melted, the sea rose by about a hundred metres in a few thousand years. Coastal plains were flooded, and about 8,000 years ago Britain became an island.

In some places, wild food was so rich that people did not need to move. The Natufians, who lived in the Middle East from about 14,000 years ago, built round stone houses and gathered wild grain with flint-bladed sickles.

Burnt crumbs found in Jordan show that people were baking flat bread about 14,400 years ago, long before farming. In a cave in Israel, scientists also found traces that suggest people brewed a drink from grain, but this is less certain.

At Göbekli Tepe in Turkey, hunter-gatherers raised circles of tall stone pillars carved with foxes, snakes and birds. They did this about 11,500 years ago, before anyone farmed, and nobody is sure whether the place was a temple.

At Jericho, beside a spring in the Jordan Valley, people lived in a town with a stone wall and a tall round tower. These were built about 10,000 years ago, and they are among the oldest such structures that we know of.
About 11,000 years ago, people in the Fertile Crescent began to plant wheat, barley, peas and lentils. Over many generations they chose the plants with the best seeds, and the crops slowly changed.

Farming began on its own in several places, which shows that it was not copied from one source. In China people grew rice and millet, in Mexico maize, in New Guinea taro, in the Andes potatoes and in Africa sorghum.
Scientists do not think there was one single cause of farming. It grew slowly over thousands of years, as people spent more and more time looking after wild plants.

People also tamed animals, and in the Middle East sheep and goats became farm animals about 10,000 years ago. Cattle and pigs followed, and people learned to use these animals for meat, milk and wool, while dogs had joined them much earlier.

A field of grain could feed far more people than the same land used for hunting. However, early farmers often worked harder, ate less varied food, and were shorter and sicker than the hunters before them.

When people lived close together and near their animals, diseases could spread easily. Many illnesses, such as flu, probably came to humans from animals, and crowded villages gave them plenty of people to infect.

Among peoples who kept cattle, a gene spread that lets adults drink milk without becoming ill. This shows that our bodies can change along with our way of life, and that human evolution did not stop with the first farms.

People made clay pots to store grain and to cook in, and boiling food in a pot made some foods safe and soft. The first pots were made by hunter-gatherers in East Asia about 20,000 years ago, long before farming.

At Çatalhöyük in Turkey, thousands of people lived in a town about 9,000 years ago. The mud houses were built so close together that there were no streets, and people climbed ladders to walk across the roofs.

Farmers who grew more grain than they needed could store the extra, and stored grain was a kind of wealth. The people who controlled it often became leaders, and in this way inequality between families grew.

At Varna, in Bulgaria, graves about 6,500 years ago held thousands of gold objects, but only a few of them were so rich. This shows that some people already had far more wealth and power than their neighbours.

When land became valuable, people began to mark it with fences and to fight about who owned it. Scientists disagree about how common war was at this time, but some skeletons show that groups did sometimes attack each other.

About 7,000 years ago, people in Europe and Asia learned how to heat certain rocks until the copper in them melted. The Iceman, who died in the Alps about 5,300 years ago, was carrying a copper axe when he was found in 1991.

As farmers spread across Europe, they built great monuments of earth and stone without any writing. Stonehenge in Britain, built in stages from about 5,000 years ago, was a place where people gathered, and its huge stones came from far away.
Mesopotamia means the land between the rivers, the Tigris and the Euphrates. Rain was scarce, so farmers dug canals, and the large harvests helped the first cities to grow there.

Uruk, in southern Mesopotamia, was one of the world's first cities, and about 5,000 years ago it may have held tens of thousands of people. It had temples, workshops and a great wall, and its people did many different kinds of work.

Writing began about 5,300 years ago in Mesopotamia, and it was first used to keep accounts. The earliest tablets recorded amounts of grain, beer and cloth, because a growing city needed to remember who owed what.

Mesopotamian scribes pressed a reed into soft clay to make wedge-shaped marks, and this writing is called cuneiform. It was used for about 3,000 years, and scribes spent years at school learning the hundreds of signs.

Writing was invented again in other places, which shows that it was not copied from one source. Egyptians wrote in picture signs called hieroglyphs about 5,200 years ago, and people in China and Mexico invented their own systems.
About 4,300 years ago a priestess called Enheduanna wrote poems to a goddess in the city of Ur. She is the first author in history whose name we know, and she was the daughter of a powerful king.

The Epic of Gilgamesh tells of a king of Uruk who loses his best friend and searches for a way to live for ever. It is one of the oldest great stories, and the first tales about Gilgamesh were written down about 4,000 years ago.

Large cities needed shared rules, so about 3,700 years ago King Hammurabi of Babylon had 282 laws carved on a tall stone. The punishments were not equal for everyone, because they depended on a person's rank.

In Egypt, beside the Nile, the Great Pyramid of Giza was built about 4,500 years ago as a tomb for King Khufu. Evidence from the workers' town suggests that many of the builders were paid labourers who were fed bread and beer.

The cities of the Indus Valley, in modern Pakistan and India, flourished about 4,500 years ago. Their streets were planned in straight lines and their houses had drains, but nobody has yet been able to read their writing.

The wheel was first used about 5,500 years ago, at first for making pottery and soon afterwards for carts. A cart with wheels could carry a heavy load much farther than a person could, so trade became easier.

On the grasslands of Eurasia, people learned to ride horses, and about 4,000 years ago they built light chariots with spoked wheels. Horses changed war, travel and the way news was carried, because a rider could cover long distances very quickly.

Boats with sails were used on the Nile and on the seas around the Mediterranean from about 5,000 years ago. A ship could carry far more than a cart or a donkey, so water was the cheapest way to move goods.

About 5,000 years ago people learned that mixing copper with a little tin made bronze, which is harder than copper. Tin is rare, so people had to trade for it over long distances, and that trade connected faraway places.

Around 3,200 years ago, many great cities in the eastern Mediterranean were destroyed, and trade networks broke down. Historians think that drought, earthquakes, raiders and failing trade may all have played a part, but they still argue about the causes.

Iron came into wide use about 3,000 years ago, and it was stronger than bronze when it was hammered into shape. Iron ore is found almost everywhere, so iron tools and weapons were cheaper, and more people could own them.

About 3,000 years ago the Phoenicians, who lived on the coast of what is now Lebanon, sailed all over the Mediterranean to trade. They used a simple alphabet of 22 letters, and the Greeks later changed it into the one that we use today.

Before there were coins, people paid for things by swapping goods or by weighing out pieces of silver. Swapping was slow, because both people had to want what the other had, and weighing silver needed scales and honesty.

The first coins that we know of were made in Lydia, in modern Turkey, about 2,600 years ago. Each coin was stamped by the ruler to show its weight and value, and so a buyer did not need to weigh it every time.

About 1,000 years ago, during the Song dynasty, China began to print paper money. Paper has almost no value in itself, so money like this works only because people trust the government and one another.
An empire is a state that rules many different peoples, often by force. The first one we know of was founded by Sargon of Akkad in Mesopotamia about 4,300 years ago.

Large empires such as Persia, Rome and Qin China used roads, messengers and armies to rule huge areas. The Persian Royal Road ran about 2,700 kilometres, and messengers changed horses at stations along the way.
Alexander the Great, a king from Macedonia in Greece, conquered a huge area from Greece to India. He died young, in 323 BCE, about 2,300 years ago, and his generals divided his empire.

Ashoka ruled most of India about 2,300 years ago, and he won a terrible war in the east of the country. Afterwards he felt great sorrow, turned towards Buddhism and had messages about kindness and fairness carved on stone pillars.

In 221 BCE, China was united under the First Emperor, who made one writing system, one kind of money and one set of measures for all. He was buried near the city of Xi'an with an army of thousands of life-sized clay soldiers.

The Han dynasty followed the First Emperor, and it kept China united for about 400 years with a large army and good roads. By about 2,000 years ago, Chinese workers were making paper from rags and bark, which was much cheaper than silk.

Rome began as a small city, and it grew until it ruled all the lands around the Mediterranean Sea. The Romans built about 80,000 kilometres of good roads, so armies, traders and messengers could travel quickly.

The Romans built aqueducts to bring water to their cities, as well as public baths and huge concrete buildings. They spread the Latin language, which became the mother of Spanish, French, Italian and other languages.

Roman wealth depended on slavery, and millions of people were bought, sold and forced to work. In 73 BCE a gladiator named Spartacus led a large revolt of enslaved people, but the Roman army defeated it.
Not every great state was in Europe or Asia, as the Maya and Aksum show. The Maya built stone cities with temples in Mexico, and Aksum, in Ethiopia, traded with Rome and India.

Around 2,500 years ago, in different parts of the world, thinkers began to ask how people should live. Confucius in China, the Buddha in India and Socrates in Greece all lived in this period, and many beliefs spread from them.

Confucius was a teacher who lived in China, and he taught that people should learn, respect their families and rule with fairness. His followers collected his sayings in a book called the Analects, and it shaped Chinese life for more than 2,000 years.

The Buddha, whose name was Siddhartha Gautama, was born as a prince in northern India. He taught that people can find peace through understanding and compassion, and Buddhism spread slowly across Asia along trade routes.

In Athens, about 2,500 years ago, citizens met in the open air to decide laws themselves, which was a new idea. However, women, enslaved people and foreigners were not citizens, so most of the people in the city had no vote.
Several of the world's great faiths grew from ancient roots. The Hebrew Bible records the belief in one God, while the oldest Hindu hymns, the Vedas, were spoken for centuries before being written.

Christianity began about 2,000 years ago in the Roman Empire, and it is based on the teachings of Jesus of Nazareth. It spread first among ordinary people, and by the fourth century it had become one of the largest religions in the empire.

Islam began in Arabia about 1,400 years ago, when Muhammad began to teach the words of the Quran in Mecca. Within a hundred years its followers had spread from Spain in the west to the edge of India in the east.

Faiths travelled along trade routes with merchants, monks and pilgrims, and they gave people shared stories and rules. They often taught charity and care for strangers, although religious differences have also been a cause of conflict and suffering.

From about 2,100 years ago, roads and sea routes linked China with the Mediterranean, and later people called them the Silk Road. Traders carried silk, spices, paper and ideas, but they also carried diseases.

Sailors learned that the monsoon winds blow in one direction for half the year and in the other direction for the rest. Using them, traders crossed the Indian Ocean regularly, linking Arabia, India, East Africa and China.

In Baghdad, about 1,200 years ago, scholars gathered in a House of Wisdom and translated Greek, Persian and Indian books into Arabic. They also added new ideas of their own in mathematics, astronomy and medicine.

Mathematicians in India treated zero as a true number, and scholars in Baghdad spread the idea. One of them, al-Khwarizmi, wrote a famous book on solving equations, and his work gave us the words algebra and algorithm.

About 1,000 years ago the scholar Ibn al-Haytham tested how light and sight work by doing experiments, which was a new way to find the truth. The doctor Ibn Sina wrote a medical encyclopaedia that was used in Asia and Europe for hundreds of years.

Chinese inventors made paper, printed books, gunpowder and the magnetic compass long before they reached Europe. The earliest dated printed book, a Buddhist text called the Diamond Sutra, was made in China in the year 868.

In 1324 Mansa Musa, the king of Mali in West Africa, made a famous pilgrimage to Mecca with so much gold that prices rose in Cairo. His kingdom grew rich from gold and salt, and the city of Timbuktu became a centre of books and teaching.

In the Andes, the Inca ruled by roads, runners and knotted cords called quipu, which were used to record numbers. In Mexico, the Aztec built Tenochtitlan on an island in a lake, and it became one of the largest cities in the world.

Polynesian sailors crossed the vast Pacific Ocean in double canoes, finding their way by the stars, the waves and the flight of birds. They reached Hawaii, Easter Island and New Zealand, which was one of the last large lands to be settled by people.

The Vikings came from Scandinavia and raided, traded and settled across Europe from about the year 800. Some of them sailed to Iceland and Greenland, and about 1,000 years ago a few even reached Newfoundland in North America.

In medieval Europe, most people were poor farmers who lived in villages. Monasteries kept old books safe by copying them, and the first universities opened in places such as Bologna and Oxford during the 1100s.

In the 1200s the Mongols, under Genghis Khan and his family, built the largest land empire in history. They destroyed many cities, including Baghdad in 1258, but they also kept the roads safe for traders and travellers.
The Black Death was caused by a germ that lived in fleas, which in turn lived on rats. It spread from Asia along the trade routes, and in 1347 it reached Europe on ships that came from the Black Sea.

Between 1347 and 1351, the Black Death swept across Europe, and it may have killed a third or more of all the people. It also reached the Middle East and North Africa, and whole villages were left empty.

With so many workers dead, the survivors could ask for higher pay, and landowners had to pay them. In western Europe, many peasants gained more freedom, although in England a revolt in 1381 showed how angry people still were.

People did not understand germs, so they argued about the cause and some blamed innocent groups, especially Jewish communities, who were attacked. Some port cities, such as Dubrovnik, made ships wait for a month or more, and this gave us the word quarantine.

In the Italian cities of the 1400s, rich merchants and bankers paid artists, architects and scholars. This led to the Renaissance, a rebirth of art and of interest in the learning of Greece and Rome, and painters learned to show depth.

Between 1405 and 1433, the Chinese admiral Zheng He led seven great voyages with hundreds of ships, some of them far larger than any in Europe. His fleets reached India, Arabia and East Africa, but afterwards China chose to end such expeditions.

About 1450, a goldsmith named Johannes Gutenberg built a printing press in the German city of Mainz. It used small metal letters that could be arranged in any order, while before then every book had to be copied by hand.

Printing with movable type was not invented only once, for Korean printers used metal type in 1377 and Chinese printers used clay type about 1040. In Europe the alphabet has few letters, so the system suited it well, and presses spread quickly.

By 1500, millions of books had been printed in Europe, and printing helped ideas spread faster than ever before. When Martin Luther criticised the Church in 1517, his writings were printed and read all over Germany within weeks.

In 1453 the Ottoman army used huge cannons to break the walls of Constantinople, which had stood strong for a thousand years. After this, gunpowder weapons changed how wars were fought, and rulers needed money to buy them.

In the 1400s sailors from Portugal explored the west coast of Africa in small ships called caravels. They used compasses and better maps, and they hoped to find a sea route to the spices and gold of Asia.

In 1498 the Portuguese captain Vasco da Gama sailed around the southern tip of Africa and reached India. This sea route let Europeans trade directly with Asia, without paying the merchants who controlled the old land routes.

In 1492 Christopher Columbus, who sailed for the rulers of Spain, crossed the Atlantic Ocean and landed in the Bahamas. He thought that he had reached Asia, but he had come to a continent where millions of people already lived.

In 1519 a Spanish fleet led by Ferdinand Magellan set out to find a western route to Asia. Magellan was killed in the Philippines in 1521, and only one ship and about 18 men returned to Spain in 1522 after sailing right around the world.

After 1492, crops, animals and diseases began to cross the oceans in both directions, in what historians call the Columbian exchange. It changed what people ate and how they lived, but it also brought terrible suffering to the Americas.

Potatoes, maize, tomatoes and chocolate went from the Americas to the rest of the world, and they helped to feed more people. Horses, cattle, wheat and sugar went the other way, and horses changed life on the grasslands of North America.
