In 1521 a small Spanish army, with the help of thousands of local allies and an outbreak of smallpox, overthrew the Aztec empire in Mexico. About ten years later Francisco Pizarro and his men took over the Inca empire in Peru, which was weakened by civil war and disease.

In 1545 Spanish miners found a mountain of silver at Potosí, in what is now Bolivia. The silver was shipped to Europe and China, so for the first time money from one continent paid for goods on another.

From the 1500s to the 1800s, more than 10 million people were taken from Africa and forced to work as slaves in the Americas. They grew sugar, cotton and tobacco on plantations, and the trade made many European merchants rich while destroying African families.

In 1602 the Dutch East India Company sold shares to the public, which allowed ordinary people to own part of a trading business. Companies like this had their own ships and soldiers, and they became powerful players in global trade.

In 1543 a Polish scholar named Nicolaus Copernicus published the idea that the Earth moves around the Sun. This challenged the old belief, held for centuries, that the Earth stood still at the centre of everything.

From the 1500s a new way of finding out spread across Europe, based on careful observation and experiment instead of old authority. In 1610 Galileo used a telescope to see the moons of Jupiter, which showed that not everything circled the Earth.

In 1633 a Church court forced Galileo to say that the Earth does not move, because they believed his ideas went against the Bible. He spent the rest of his life under house arrest, but his books continued to be read.
The microscope opened up a hidden world that nobody had known before. In 1665 Robert Hooke named the cells he saw in cork, and soon afterwards Leeuwenhoek found tiny living things in pond water.

In 1687 Isaac Newton published a book that showed how one law of gravity explains why an apple falls and why the Moon circles the Earth. It suggested that the same simple laws work everywhere in the universe.

Scientists began to share their work in societies and journals, where others could test and correct it. Science grew because people admitted when they were wrong, and a claim had to be backed by evidence, not just by someone's rank.

In the 1700s writers in Europe argued for reason, free speech and human rights, and this period is called the Enlightenment. Their ideas inspired the American Revolution of 1776 and the French Revolution of 1789.

In the late 1700s a movement to end the slave trade grew in Britain, led by religious groups and by freed slaves. Britain banned the trade in 1807 and ended slavery in its empire in 1833, and the United States ended it in 1865.

In 1859 Charles Darwin published On the Origin of Species, which explained evolution by natural selection. He showed that all living things, including humans, share common ancestors, and the idea changed biology for ever.

Women were often shut out of universities, but many of them contributed to science. Maria Sibylla Merian painted and studied insects in Suriname, and Émilie du Châtelet translated Newton's work into French and explained it.
From about 1760, Britain began to use coal, steam engines and machines in large factories. The cotton industry grew very fast, and many people left the countryside to find work in the new towns.

Coal is energy that was stored by plants millions of years ago, and burning it makes heat. Steam engines used it to do work that once needed many people and animals, and James Watt greatly improved them in the 1760s.

Cities grew at an astonishing speed, and by about 1800 London had more than a million people. Many streets were crowded and dirty, and diseases such as cholera spread easily where there was no clean water.
Factory work was long and hard, and children worked in mills and mines for very little money. Over many years, new laws and workers' unions slowly improved conditions, and wages began to rise.

In the 1800s, railways made travel much faster than a horse could, and the first passenger railway opened in England in 1825. Trains carried people, food and goods across whole countries, and towns near the stations grew rich.

The telegraph sent messages along wires in moments, and it was first used in 1844 with Samuel Morse's code. After some early failures, a lasting cable crossed the Atlantic Ocean in 1866, so news from America reached Europe in minutes.
Electricity changed homes and factories, and practical electric lamps appeared in the 1870s. Soon cities had power stations and telephones, and the evening was no longer ruled by the dark.

In 1885 Karl Benz built one of the first petrol cars in Germany. Henry Ford's assembly line, which began in 1913, made cars so cheap that ordinary families could buy them, and it changed the shape of cities.

The human population passed one billion about 1800, which had taken our species hundreds of thousands of years. After that, it grew faster and faster, with two billion by 1927, four billion by 1974 and eight billion in 2022.

By 1914 European states ruled most of Africa and large parts of Asia, and they usually did not ask the people who lived there. These empires took raw materials and sometimes forced people to work, and many peoples resisted them.

For most of history many children died young, and the average life was short because of this. In about 1800 more than four in ten children died before the age of five, but today the figure is about four in a hundred.

In 1796 an English doctor named Edward Jenner showed that people who caught a mild illness called cowpox did not catch smallpox. He used this to make the first vaccine, and the word comes from the Latin word for cow.

Smallpox killed hundreds of millions of people over the centuries, and many survivors were left scarred or blind. After a worldwide campaign of vaccination, the disease was wiped out by 1980, and it is the only human disease so far to be removed completely.

In the 1800s doctors began to find out that tiny living things called germs cause many diseases. Ignaz Semmelweis showed that washing hands saved mothers' lives, and later Louis Pasteur and Robert Koch proved the germ theory.

Clean water and sewers did more to save lives than almost any medicine, because they stopped diseases such as cholera. After a terrible smell from the River Thames in 1858, London built a huge sewer system, and cities all over the world copied it.

In 1928 Alexander Fleming noticed that a mould had killed the bacteria around it in a dish in his laboratory. Other scientists made it into the drug penicillin, and antibiotics now cure many infections, although some germs are learning to resist them.

In the early 1900s two German chemists, Fritz Haber and Carl Bosch, found a way to make fertiliser from nitrogen in the air. Many experts think that about half of the people alive today eat food that was grown with it.

In the 1960s the scientist Norman Borlaug and his colleagues bred short, strong wheat that gave far bigger harvests. It was grown widely in Mexico, India and Pakistan, and many experts believe it saved millions of people from hunger.
Life has improved for a great number of people over the past 200 years, although many are still poor. In 1820 about eight in ten people lived in extreme poverty, but today fewer than one in ten do.

As more children survived, and as women gained education and rights, parents began to have fewer children. Families grew smaller, and the growth of the world's population began to slow, even though the total is still rising.

The First World War, from 1914 to 1918, was the first war fought with weapons made in great factories, such as machine guns and poison gas. About ten million soldiers and many millions of civilians died, and the old empires of Europe fell.
In 1918 and 1919 a flu pandemic spread around the world on ships and trains, while the war was ending. Scientists estimate that about 50 million people died, which was more than the war itself.

The Second World War, from 1939 to 1945, killed tens of millions of people and was the deadliest war in history. Six million Jews, along with many other people, were murdered by Nazi Germany in the Holocaust.

In 1945 the first atomic bombs were used on two cities in Japan, and the war ended soon afterwards. Since then nuclear weapons have become much more powerful, and the fear of a nuclear war was a part of life for decades.

In 1945 the United Nations was founded to help keep the peace, and in 1948 it published a list of human rights for all people. After the war many colonies became independent, starting with India in 1947 and many African countries in the 1960s.

In 1903 two brothers, Wilbur and Orville Wright, made the first powered flight in a small plane at Kitty Hawk in the United States. It lasted only twelve seconds, but within a lifetime jet planes were carrying millions of people across the world.
In 1957 the Soviet Union launched Sputnik, the first satellite to orbit the Earth. In 1961 Yuri Gagarin travelled around the Earth in a spacecraft, and he became the first person in space.

In July 1969 the American spacecraft Apollo 11 landed on the Moon, and Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin walked on its surface. Only 66 years had passed since the first short flight of the Wright brothers.

In 1968 astronauts in orbit around the Moon took a famous photograph of the Earth rising above the grey surface. The picture showed how small and fragile our planet is, and it helped to inspire the first Earth Day in 1970.

The first computers filled whole rooms, but after the invention of the transistor and the chip they became smaller and cheaper. The World Wide Web began about 1990, and today more than five billion people use the internet.
Burning coal, oil and gas adds carbon dioxide to the air, and this gas traps heat. Since the 1800s the planet has warmed by a little more than one degree Celsius.

A warmer world brings stronger heat waves, droughts and floods, and the sea is slowly rising as ice melts. In 2015 nearly every country agreed in Paris to try to limit the warming, but many scientists say that more must be done.

Humans and the animals that we keep for food now make up most of the weight of all the mammals on Earth. Wild mammals are only a small fraction, and many wild species are in danger as forests are cut and their homes shrink.

The last passenger pigeon, a bird that was once among the most common in North America, died in a zoo in 1914. Scientists warn that up to a million species of plants and animals may be at risk of dying out.
People can solve shared problems when they work together. A world treaty in 1987 stopped chemicals that harmed the ozone layer, and a ban on whale hunting is helping some whales return.

Energy from the sun and the wind has become much cheaper in the past fifteen years. Many countries are now building more solar panels and wind farms each year, which gives hope of using less coal, oil and gas.

In 2003 scientists finished reading the full human genome, which is the complete set of instructions in our DNA. They found that any two people are almost exactly the same, and the differences between us are tiny compared with what we share.

New tools, such as gene editing and artificial intelligence, give people great power, and they can do much good. Societies must decide how to use them wisely, and ordinary people, not only experts, have a part in those choices.

Humans took over the world not because we were the strongest, but because we learned to share what we know. Language, writing, trade, science and the internet let each generation build on the work of the last.
All people alive today belong to one species, and our genes are almost the same. The story is not finished, and the choices we make will shape the next chapter.
C1C2: Among the millions of species that share this planet, we are neither the strongest, nor the fastest, nor the oldest. And yet, in a very short span of time, we have built cities, filled the sky with aircraft and left our footprints on the Moon. This book follows that long and surprising journey, from a small group of people in Africa to a world of eight billion.

Our planet formed about four and a half billion years ago, and the first simple living things appeared in its oceans more than three and a half billion years ago. For most of that immense stretch of time there were no animals with bones, no forests and certainly no people. If the entire history of Earth were squeezed into a single day, our species would not appear until the last few seconds before midnight.

About 66 million years ago a vast rock from space struck the Earth, and the climate changed so sharply that the great dinosaurs, apart from the birds, died out. Small mammals that had scurried in their shadow suddenly found the world open to them. Over millions of years they spread into forests, grasslands and seas, and among their many descendants were the first primates.

Primates, the group of mammals that includes monkeys, apes and humans, developed flexible hands for gripping branches and forward-facing eyes that judge distance well. Their brains are large for their body size, and most of them live in close-knit social groups. Much of what a young primate needs to know is learned by watching and copying the adults around it.

Humans are not something apart from the animal world: we are one of the great apes, alongside gorillas, orangutans, chimpanzees and bonobos. Our closest living relatives are the chimpanzees and bonobos, and their DNA is strikingly similar to ours. Studying how they live gives scientists clues about how our own ancestors may have behaved.

According to the evidence from fossils and DNA, humans and chimpanzees share a common ancestor that lived in Africa about six to seven million years ago. Its descendants slowly drifted apart into two separate lines, as small differences in how they lived added up over many generations. One line led to the chimpanzees and bonobos of today, and the other led, after a very long road, to us.

At a place called Laetoli, in Tanzania, a small group of early human relatives walked across fresh volcanic ash more than three and a half million years ago. Rain dampened the ash, which then dried hard, and the footprints lay preserved until scientists discovered them in the twentieth century. They show clearly that these creatures walked upright on two legs, with a stride not so different from our own.

Nobody knows for certain why our ancestors began to walk on two legs, and scientists have proposed many explanations, from saving energy on long journeys to wading through shallow water. Whatever the reason, the change had huge consequences, because it left the hands free to carry food, tools and children. Over millions of years those hands would become the most skilful instruments on the planet.

In 1974 a team of scientists working in the dry hills of Ethiopia found about forty per cent of the skeleton of a small adult who had lived roughly three million years ago. They named her Lucy, after a song that was playing in their camp, and she belonged to a species called Australopithecus afarensis. Lucy stood just over a metre tall and her brain was no larger than a chimpanzee's, yet she walked upright.

By about two and a half million years ago, some of our relatives in Africa had learned to strike one stone against another and break off sharp flakes. These simple tools, though crude, could slice meat from the bodies of dead animals and crack open bones to reach the rich marrow inside. Using them gave early toolmakers a new source of food, and it rewarded those with clever hands and quick minds.

Somewhere between two and three million years ago, a new group of early humans appeared in Africa, and scientists give it the name Homo, which is simply the Latin word for human. One of its first members, Homo habilis, had a brain noticeably larger than Lucy's and made stone tools with growing skill. Its name means handy man, and it marks the start of the long family that led to us.

Nearly two million years ago a taller and more athletic kind of human, Homo erectus, appeared in Africa, with long legs and a body built for covering great distances on foot. A famous skeleton of a boy, found near Lake Turkana in Kenya and about 1,500,000 years old, shows a frame that looks strikingly modern from the neck down. The species proved so successful that it survived for well over a million years, far longer than our own has existed so far.

Homo erectus made hand axes by chipping both sides of a stone until it had a keen, symmetrical, teardrop-shaped edge, and this useful design appeared about 1,700,000 years ago. Astonishingly, people kept making almost the same tool for more than a million years, across Africa, Europe and Asia. The patience and the sense of form that each axe required suggest that skills were taught carefully from one generation to the next.

Homo erectus was the first human to leave Africa, and the evidence includes remarkable skulls found at Dmanisi in Georgia, which are about 1,800,000 years old. Over many generations their descendants spread eastward across Asia, following rivers and coasts, and their remains have been found as far away as Java and China. These travellers did not set out to explore the world, but each generation simply moved a little farther in search of food.

At some point our ancestors learned to control fire, which gave them warmth, light and protection from predators. Scientists disagree about when this momentous step happened, but burnt bones and ash in Wonderwerk Cave in South Africa show that fire was in use about a million years ago. It remains uncertain when people first learned to start a fire at will, instead of keeping one alive after lightning had lit it.

Fire kept dangerous animals away from the sleeping camp, and it stretched the day, turning the dark hours into a time for talking, mending tools and sharing food. People also learned that holding the point of a wooden spear in the flames made it harder and sharper. A fire in the middle of a group became a natural meeting place, and some scientists think it strengthened the bonds between people.

Cooking made food softer and far easier to digest, so the body needed much less energy to break it down. Some scientists believe this helped to feed the human brain, which uses about a fifth of the body's energy although it weighs only a small fraction as much. The idea is debated, because no one can say exactly when cooking became a regular habit.

Over about two million years the human brain grew to roughly three times the size of Lucy's, and that growth came at a price. Human babies were born helpless compared with young apes, and they needed years of care, so groups that shared the work of feeding and protecting their children were more likely to flourish. Cooperation, in other words, was not an extra for early humans but a matter of survival.

In a marsh at Schöningen in Germany, hunters about 300,000 years ago made beautiful throwing spears from spruce wood, carefully shaped so that they were heavier towards the front like a modern javelin. The bones of butchered wild horses were found close by, and they suggest that the hunters planned an ambush and worked together. Such finds show that early humans were not simple brutes, but skilful planners who thought ahead and worked together to feed their families.

By about 300,000 years ago, the descendants of earlier humans lived across Africa, Europe and Asia, and they were slowly becoming different from one another in each region. Studies of ancient DNA suggest that the ancestors of the Neanderthals and of our own species separated some time between 500,000 and 700,000 years ago. One branch settled in the cold lands of Europe, while the other remained in Africa and would eventually become us.

The oldest known bones that look like ours were found at Jebel Irhoud in Morocco, and a new dating method showed that they are about 300,000 years old. The faces of these people already resembled ours, with small brow ridges and a flat face, although their skulls were still long and low. Over many thousands of years the shape of the skull slowly became rounder, and that change marks the rise of Homo sapiens.

Other very old bones, from Ethiopia and from South Africa, show that Homo sapiens developed in many parts of the African continent rather than in one single valley. Groups probably met, traded and married across large distances, so that useful ideas and genes passed between them. Our origin, in other words, may have been less like a single birth and more like a river made of many streams.

Neanderthals were strong, stocky people with wide noses and powerful arms, well suited to the cold climates of Europe and western Asia, where they lived for more than 300,000 years. Their brains were as large as ours, and they hunted big animals such as deer, wild horses and even mammoths. Far from being the dim brutes of old cartoons, they were skilful and adaptable survivors of a harsh world.

Neanderthals made fire, wooden spears and stone tools, and they produced a sticky glue from birch tar to fix sharp stones to wooden handles. A skeleton found in Shanidar Cave in Iraq shows that a man with serious injuries survived for years, which suggests that others looked after him. Care for the weak seems to have been part of Neanderthal life, just as it is part of ours.

A few discoveries, including red marks in Spanish caves and pierced shells used as ornaments, hint that Neanderthals may also have made symbols. Many scientists accept this, but others argue that the dates are doubtful or that the objects were made by our own species. The question is still open, and each new find, rather than settling it, tends to make it more interesting.

In 2010 scientists extracted DNA from a tiny finger bone found in Denisova Cave in Siberia, and to their astonishment it matched neither Neanderthals nor modern humans. It revealed a previously unknown group of people, now called the Denisovans, who lived across parts of Asia. We know them mostly from a few bones and teeth, but their genes have survived in people alive today.

On the island of Flores in Indonesia, scientists discovered the bones of adults who stood only a little over a metre tall and had small brains. They are called Homo floresiensis, or the hobbit, and they may have survived there until about 50,000 years ago. Some researchers think they descended from earlier humans who became smaller over time, a common pattern among animals that live on islands.

In a deep cave system in South Africa, explorers squeezed through a narrow crack to find the bones of a small-brained human called Homo naledi. Careful dating showed that it lived about 300,000 years ago, at the same time as the earliest Homo sapiens, which surprised many experts. It proves that the human family tree was far bushier than anyone had expected.

At sites in Kenya, people about 300,000 years ago carried black volcanic glass and red pigments over many miles from where they were found. This suggests that separate groups traded or at least met, and contact of that kind would have spread new ideas and helped communities to survive bad times. Even at this early stage, human networks reached beyond the horizon of a single band.

For most of its history our species shared the world with other kinds of human, including Neanderthals, Denisovans and several small groups in Asia and Africa. Why we alone survived is one of the great questions of science, and nobody has found a single answer that satisfies everyone. The story of the next few chapters is partly an attempt to look at the clues.

For almost the whole of human history, people lived in small bands of a few dozen individuals, moving with the seasons to follow fruit, fish and the migrating herds. They owned only what they could carry, and the wide world around them was both their home and their larder. Everything that we now call civilisation grew out of this long and mobile way of life.

Foragers gathered fruit, nuts, roots and honey, and they hunted animals and caught fish, depending on the place and the time of year. Who did which task varied from one community to another, and both women and men probably possessed deep knowledge of the plants and animals around them. No single rule applied everywhere, and we should be careful of simple stories about the past.

Some scientists study modern foraging peoples, such as the Hadza of Tanzania, in order to understand how early bands may have lived. These groups share food widely and do not allow any one person to gain too much power, and it is possible that many of our ancestors lived in the same spirit. We cannot be sure, however, because societies change, and the present is never a perfect mirror of the past.

A band's survival depended upon a store of knowledge about where water could be found, which plants were safe and how each animal behaved in each season. Children learned this inheritance by watching and listening to stories, by joining in songs and games, and by sharing the daily work. Because nothing could be written down, memory and the spoken word were the library of the human race.

Nobody knows when language began, because speech leaves no fossils, and scientists argue about whether it appeared slowly or in a sudden leap. What is certain is that language allowed people to warn each other of danger, to teach skills, to make plans and to describe things that were not in front of them. With words, the knowledge of one clever person could become the property of the whole band.

In Blombos Cave on the coast of South Africa, people at least 75,000 years ago strung beads made from tiny sea shells and scratched careful patterns onto pieces of red ochre. These objects are among the earliest signs that humans used symbols to show who they were and where they belonged. Anyone who wears a ring or a team shirt today is following the same ancient habit.

Fine bone needles, some about 40,000 years old, have been found in Siberia and elsewhere, and they show that people were sewing clothes from animal skins. Warm and well-fitted clothing allowed our ancestors to survive in cold lands where no human had ever lived before. Without it, the great migrations into northern Europe and Asia would hardly have been possible.

At least 40,000 years ago people began to paint animals and red handprints on the walls of caves, working by the flickering light of torches. The oldest known painting of an animal, a wild pig, was discovered on the Indonesian island of Sulawesi, and it is about 45,000 years old. Whoever made these images understood that a picture could stand for something that was not there.

In caves in southern Germany, archaeologists found flutes made from the hollow bones of birds and from mammoth ivory, and they are about 40,000 years old. Nearby lay a small statue of a human body with a lion's head, carved with great patience from ivory. Music and imagination, it seems, are almost as ancient as the first cave paintings, and perhaps as old as language itself.

Some ancient graves, such as those at Sunghir in Russia, hold thousands of ivory beads and carefully made ornaments that were buried with the dead. Such burials show that people took great care of those who had died, and many scholars believe they reflect early beliefs about death. We can only guess what the mourners thought, since no one left a written word.

A few groups of Homo sapiens left Africa long before the main migration, as a jawbone found in Misliya Cave in Israel shows, for it is about 180,000 years old. Other early travellers have left their bones in the same region, and the evidence suggests that several small waves of people moved out of Africa. Those pioneers seem to have died out or to have been absorbed by other groups, leaving few traces in our DNA.

The great spread of our species across the world seems to have begun about 60,000 to 70,000 years ago, and it is the journey that matters most for the story of humankind. The travellers who left Africa then were the ancestors of almost everyone who lives outside Africa today. It was not an organised expedition with a leader and a map, but a slow drift of families into country that nobody had seen before.

About 74,000 years ago a giant volcano erupted at Toba in Sumatra, throwing so much ash into the sky that it covered much of southern Asia. Scientists disagree about how greatly the disaster affected human groups, and some argue that the damage was small. It is a reminder that the human story has often been shaped by forces beyond anyone's control.

The sea shore offered a steady supply of shellfish, fish and seabirds, so food was easier to find there than inland. Groups may have followed the coasts of Arabia and southern Asia, moving perhaps only a few kilometres in each generation. Over thousands of years, such small steps carried their descendants across a continent without any single person ever making a long journey.

When our ancestors reached Europe and Asia, they met the Neanderthals and Denisovans, and the different groups lived side by side for thousands of years. We do not know how they treated one another, and the truth was probably varied, with fear, trade and friendship in different places. Whatever happened in each place, the meetings left their mark in a very personal way, as the next page will show.

Ancient DNA has revealed that our ancestors sometimes had children with Neanderthals and Denisovans, and that those children were raised within modern human groups. As a result, many people today carry a small share of their DNA, usually between one and two per cent in people from Europe or Asia. A part of those lost cousins therefore lives on in us, and it is even doing useful work in some bodies.

Many Tibetans carry a gene that came from the Denisovans, and it helps the body to cope with the thin air of the high mountains. This is a striking example of how a gene from another human group, acquired thousands of years ago, can still be useful today. Our species, it seems, borrowed far more than anyone imagined from its relatives, and the borrowing was sometimes of lasting benefit.

In Denisova Cave, scientists found a tiny bone that belonged to a teenage girl who died about 90,000 years ago. Her DNA showed that her mother was a Neanderthal and her father was a Denisovan, and she is nicknamed Denny. She is the first known child of two different kinds of ancient human, and her bone proves that such meetings did happen.

The Neanderthals died out about 40,000 years ago, and the other human species disappeared as well, so that our own became the only one left. Climate change, disease, small populations and competition with our own species have all been suggested, but scientists do not agree on the cause. It may well have been a combination of reasons, which differed from place to place.

People reached Australia at least 50,000 years ago, and some researchers think it may have been much earlier. To get there they had to cross open sea in boats or rafts, since the land was never joined to Asia, so they must have been skilled and daring sailors. The Aboriginal peoples of Australia today have one of the oldest continuing cultures in the world.

About 26,000 to 20,000 years ago the last Ice Age reached its coldest point, and thick sheets of ice spread over much of North America and northern Europe. So much of the planet's water was locked up as ice that the sea stood more than a hundred metres lower than it does today. Coastlines were therefore very different from those of today, and many places that now lie under the sea were then dry land.

In the open plains of eastern Europe, Ice Age hunters built houses from the bones and tusks of mammoths, which they covered with animal skins to keep out the wind. They wore carefully sewn clothes and heated their homes with small fires, and some camps were used year after year, because herds of animals returned each season. Survival in such a harsh world demanded great skill, careful planning and constant cooperation between neighbours.

Ice Age people carved small figures of women from stone, bone and ivory, and the best known, the Venus of Willendorf, is about 30,000 years old. Nobody knows what these figures meant to those who made them, and archaeologists have suggested everything from good-luck charms to portraits. What is certain is that people, even in the middle of an Ice Age, had the time and the imagination to create objects that were beautiful.

In the cave of Lascaux, in southern France, people painted more than a thousand horses, bulls and deer about 17,000 years ago. They ground coloured earth into powder, mixed it with water or fat, and worked by the light of small stone lamps in the darkness of the cave. The paintings still seem remarkably fresh, and they show an astonishing eye for movement.

Dogs are descended from wolves, and they were probably the first animals that people ever tamed, possibly because wolves came to scavenge around human camps. DNA suggests that dogs were living with people at least 15,000 years ago, and some scientists believe the partnership began far earlier. In one German grave about 14,000 years old, a dog was buried beside two people, which suggests that it was treasured.

When the sea was low, a broad land called Beringia joined Siberia to Alaska, and it was a cold, windy place with grass, animals and few trees. Some scientists think that groups of people lived there for thousands of years, adapting to the cold, before moving south. Today the land lies beneath the sea, which makes it hard for archaeologists to search for evidence.

During the last Ice Age the low sea opened a route between Siberia and Alaska, and groups of people made their way into the Americas, a continent that no human had ever seen. Most scientists agree that people had arrived by about 15,000 years ago, although the exact date is still debated. Some may have travelled along the coast by boat, while others walked on foot through the cold open country between the ice sheets.

Human footprints pressed into the mud beside an ancient lake in New Mexico are probably between 21,000 and 23,000 years old, according to recent studies. If the dating is right, people reached the Americas thousands of years earlier than most scientists had believed, which would change the story of the first Americans. The result is still being tested by other teams of scientists, which is exactly how good science should work.

As people spread across the world, many giant animals died out, including mammoths, giant ground sloths and huge kangaroos. Scientists think that hunting and a changing climate both played a part, but they still debate which one mattered more in each place. It is possible that people, even in small numbers, tipped over the edge animals that were already struggling to survive in a changing world.

New tools made hunting and fishing easier, and among them were spear-throwers, which allowed a hunter to throw a spear much farther and harder than by hand. Bows, nets and fish hooks followed, and with them people could catch more food and feed larger groups. Each invention was only a small step, but together they gave humans a growing advantage over the animals that they hunted.

About 11,700 years ago the last Ice Age ended, and the world became warmer and wetter, with a climate that was far steadier than anything people had known for tens of thousands of years. Earlier, the weather had swung wildly between cold and warm, which made planting crops a gamble no one could afford. With the new, kinder climate, those who tended wild plants could count on the seasons far more reliably.

As the great ice sheets melted, the sea rose by about a hundred metres over several thousand years, and it drowned wide plains where hunters had once followed the herds. The land bridge to Alaska vanished, and about 8,000 years ago the rising water cut Britain off from the rest of Europe and made it an island. Whole landscapes where people once hunted, fished and raised their children now lie hidden beneath the waves of the North Sea and many other seas.

In some places, wild food was so plentiful that people no longer needed to move. The Natufians, who lived in the Middle East from about 14,000 years ago, built round stone houses, harvested wild grain with sickles made of flint blades and ground it into flour. They were settled villagers long before anyone had planted a single field, which overturns the old idea that only farming made people stay in one place.

Burnt crumbs found at a site in Jordan show that people were baking flat bread about 14,400 years ago, thousands of years before the first farms. In a cave in Israel, scientists have also found traces that suggest people brewed a drink from grain, although the evidence is less certain. Both finds suggest that cereals were valued as food long before they were grown.

At Göbekli Tepe in Turkey, hunter-gatherers raised great circles of stone pillars, some taller than a house, and carved them with foxes, snakes, boars and birds. They did this about 11,500 years ago, before anyone had farmed, and nobody is sure whether the site was a temple, a meeting place or something else. It proves that large communities could organise themselves to build monuments without the help of agriculture.

At Jericho, beside a spring in the Jordan Valley, people built a town with a stone wall and a tall round tower about 10,000 years ago. These structures are among the oldest of their kind that we know, and building them must have required hundreds of people to work together. It is a sign that the more settled life of villages was already leading people towards the first towns.

About 11,000 years ago, people in the Fertile Crescent, an arc of land stretching from modern Egypt to Iraq, began to plant wheat, barley, peas and lentils. Over many generations they chose the plants with the best seeds, so the crops slowly changed and became more useful to humans. The change was so gradual that no one living at the time could have noticed it happening.

Farming did not begin in just one place, which shows that it was not copied from a single source. In China people grew rice and millet, in Mexico they grew maize, in New Guinea taro and bananas, in the Andes potatoes and in Africa sorghum and yams. Different peoples, living on different continents and facing similar problems, arrived at a similar solution.

Scientists do not think that one single cause explains the beginning of farming, and several ideas are still discussed. It was a slow change over thousands of years, as people spent more and more time looking after wild plants, and a growing population or a changing climate may have pushed them. There was no day on which hunters became farmers, only a long path in which the balance gradually shifted.

People also tamed animals, and in the Middle East sheep and goats became farm animals about 10,000 years ago. Cattle and pigs followed, and people learned to use these animals for meat, milk and wool, while dogs had joined them much earlier. Keeping animals gave farmers a store of food that could walk and even grow, and it was the start of a close and unequal partnership.

A field of grain could feed far more people than the same land used for hunting, and that is why farming spread so widely. However, early farmers often worked harder, ate a less varied diet, and were shorter and less healthy than the hunters who came before them, as their bones show. In a hard bargain, people gained numbers and safety from hunger, but they lost leisure and variety.

When people lived close together and near their animals, diseases found it easy to spread. Many illnesses, such as influenza, probably came to humans from animals, and crowded villages gave new germs plenty of people to infect. Epidemics that were unknown among scattered bands of hunters became a regular danger to settled farmers.

Among peoples who kept cattle, sheep or goats, a gene spread that lets adults drink milk without becoming ill. This shows that our bodies can change along with our way of life, and that human evolution did not stop with the first farms. A habit of culture had become a force in the natural selection of our genes.

People made clay pots to store grain and to cook in, and boiling food in a pot made many tough or poisonous foods safe and soft. The first pots were made by hunter-gatherers in East Asia about 20,000 years ago, long before farming began. Pots only became common, however, when people settled in villages, because clay jars are heavy and difficult to carry from camp to camp.

At Çatalhöyük in Turkey, thousands of people lived together in a town about 9,000 years ago. The mud houses were built so close together that there were no streets, and people climbed ladders and walked across the flat roofs to reach their front doors. Inside, families painted the walls, and they often buried their dead beneath the floors of their own homes.

Farmers who grew more grain than they needed could store the extra, and stored grain was a kind of wealth that could be saved, guarded and traded. The people who controlled the stores often became leaders, and over time their families passed power on to their children. In this way inequality grew, as some households became wealthy while others depended on them.

At Varna, in Bulgaria, graves from about 6,500 years ago held thousands of gold ornaments, which are among the oldest worked gold ever found. Only a few of the graves were so rich, however, while most held very little, which shows that some people already had far more wealth and prestige than their neighbours. The burial ground gives a glimpse of the world where ranks were taking shape.

When land became valuable, people began to mark it with fences and ditches and to argue about who owned it. Scientists disagree about how common war was at this time, but some mass graves, such as one in Germany, show that groups did sometimes attack each other. Violence was probably not new, but crowded lands and stored food gave people more to fight about.

About 7,000 years ago, people in south-eastern Europe and western Asia learned to heat certain green rocks until the copper in them melted and could be poured into moulds. The Iceman, who died in the Alps about 5,300 years ago and was found by walkers in 1991, was carrying a copper axe. Metal was a precious novelty, and those who could make it became people of great importance.

As farmers spread across Europe, they built great monuments of earth and stone without the help of writing, and some still stand today. Stonehenge in Britain, built in stages from about 5,000 years ago, was a place where people gathered, and its huge stones came from far away. How the builders moved them with only ropes, sledges and many strong people remains a source of wonder.

Mesopotamia means the land between the rivers, and it lay between the Tigris and the Euphrates in what is now Iraq. Rain was scarce, so farmers dug canals to bring the river water to their fields, and the harvests grew so large that the first cities were able to rise there. Here, as elsewhere, it was an organised effort by many people, not the work of a single clever family.

Uruk, in southern Mesopotamia, was one of the world's first cities, and about 5,000 years ago it may have held tens of thousands of people. It had temples, workshops and a great wall, and its inhabitants were no longer all farmers but included potters, builders, priests and traders. Living among thousands of strangers, rather than a few dozen relatives, was a completely new kind of human experience.

Writing began about 5,300 years ago in Mesopotamia, and it was first used for the dull but vital business of keeping accounts. The earliest tablets recorded amounts of grain, beer and cloth, because a growing city needed to remember who owed what to whom. It was a long way from poetry, but it solved a problem that the human memory could not.

Mesopotamian scribes pressed the end of a reed into soft clay to make wedge-shaped marks, and the system is called cuneiform, from a Latin word for wedge. It was used for about 3,000 years to write several different languages, and young scribes spent years in school learning the hundreds of signs. Because clay lasts almost for ever, hundreds of thousands of these tablets have survived.

Writing was invented again in other parts of the world, which shows how natural the idea was once cities existed. The Egyptians wrote in picture signs called hieroglyphs about 5,200 years ago, often on papyrus, a kind of paper made from river reeds, while people in China and in Mexico developed their own systems. None of these peoples copied from the others, and each wrote in a different way.

About 4,300 years ago a priestess called Enheduanna wrote poems of praise to a goddess, and she lived in the city of Ur in Mesopotamia. She is the first author in history whose name we know, and she was the daughter of a powerful king. Her work was copied by schoolchildren for hundreds of years, which proves how much her words were admired.

The Epic of Gilgamesh tells of a king of Uruk who befriends a wild man, mourns his death and then wanders the world in search of immortality. It is one of the oldest great stories, and the earliest tales about Gilgamesh were set down in writing about 4,000 years ago. Like many later epics, it grapples with the troubling fact that every mortal being must one day die.

Large cities needed shared rules, and some of the oldest written laws come from Mesopotamia, including a code that is about 4,100 years old. About 3,700 years ago King Hammurabi of Babylon had 282 laws carved on a tall stone for all to see, covering trade, property and family life. The punishments were not equal for everyone, however, because they depended on a person's rank.

In Egypt, beside the Nile, the Great Pyramid of Giza was built about 4,500 years ago as a tomb for the pharaoh Khufu, using more than two million blocks of stone. Evidence from the workers' town nearby suggests that many of the builders were paid labourers who were fed bread, beer and meat, rather than slaves. The pyramid is a measure of how many people a single ruler could feed and direct.

The cities of the Indus Valley, in what is now Pakistan and India, flourished about 4,500 years ago, and some of them held tens of thousands of people. Their streets were planned in straight lines, most houses had drains and goods were weighed with standard stone weights, which suggests careful government. Their writing, however, is still a mystery, and nobody has yet been able to read it.

The wheel was first used about 5,500 years ago, at first for making pottery and soon afterwards for carts, and the oldest wheel yet found comes from a marsh near Ljubljana in Slovenia. A cart with wheels could carry a heavy load much farther than a person could, and trade became easier wherever the ground was flat. Strangely, some great peoples, such as the Maya and the Inca, never used wheeled carts for transport.

On the grasslands of Eurasia, people learned to ride horses, and about 4,000 years ago they built light chariots with spoked wheels. Horses changed warfare, travel and the speed at which news could spread, because a single rider could cover in a day a distance that would have taken a walker several days. Those who owned the best horses and chariots held a decisive advantage in battle, and they often became the rulers of their neighbours.

Boats with sails were used on the Nile and on the seas around the Mediterranean from about 5,000 years ago, and later in many other parts of the world. A ship could carry far more than a cart or a donkey, so water was usually the cheapest way to move goods over a long distance. That is why so many great cities, from Ur to London, grew up beside rivers and coasts, where goods could arrive by boat.

About 5,000 years ago people discovered that mixing copper with a little tin produced bronze, a metal harder and more useful than copper alone. Tin is rare, so people had to trade for it over long distances, sometimes across hundreds of kilometres, and that demand connected faraway places. The new age of metal was therefore also an age of travel and bargaining.

Around 3,200 years ago, many great cities in the eastern Mediterranean were destroyed, trade networks broke down, and palaces and writing disappeared from some regions for centuries. Historians suggest that drought, earthquakes, raiders from the sea and failing trade may all have played a part, but they still argue about the causes. The collapse shows how easily complex societies can be shaken when many things go wrong at once.

Iron came into wide use about 3,000 years ago, and when it was properly worked it was stronger than bronze. Iron ore is found almost everywhere, unlike tin, so iron tools and weapons were cheaper, and farmers as well as soldiers could own them. Over time, the plough, the axe and the sword all changed, and with them the balance of power between rulers and ordinary people.

About 3,000 years ago the Phoenicians, who lived on the coast of what is now Lebanon, sailed all over the Mediterranean to trade in purple cloth, glass and cedar wood. They used a simple alphabet of 22 letters, each standing for a sound, and the Greeks later adapted it and added vowels. Nearly all the alphabets in Europe, including the one you are reading now, descend from it.

Before there were coins, people paid for things by swapping goods or by weighing out pieces of silver. Swapping was slow and awkward, because each person had to want exactly what the other had, while weighing silver required scales, honest dealers and plenty of time. As trade grew across wider and wider regions, merchants and rulers began looking for a form of payment that was simpler, quicker and easier to trust.

The first coins that we know of were made in Lydia, in what is now Turkey, about 2,600 years ago, from a natural mixture of gold and silver. Each coin was stamped by the ruler to show its weight and value, and so a buyer did not need to weigh it every time. Soon afterwards, the idea of coined money spread to Greece, Persia and India, and China developed its own metal coins at about the same time.

About 1,000 years ago, during the Song dynasty, China began to print paper money, centuries before Europe did so. Paper has almost no value in itself, so money like this works only because people trust the government that issues it and trust one another to accept it. In a very real sense, money is a shared belief that can link millions of strangers.

An empire is a state that rules over many different peoples, usually by force and by demanding taxes or gifts from those it has conquered. The first one we know of was founded by Sargon of Akkad in Mesopotamia about 4,300 years ago. Afterwards the pattern repeated itself on every continent, and for most of recorded history most people lived under the rule of some empire.

Large empires such as Persia, Rome and Qin China relied on roads, messengers and armies to rule huge areas. The Persian Royal Road ran for about 2,700 kilometres, and royal messengers changed horses at stations along the way so that news travelled far faster than a single rider could manage. Control of information, in other words, was as important to an empire as control of soldiers.

Alexander the Great, a young king from Macedonia in northern Greece, conquered a vast area stretching from Greece and Egypt to the edge of India. He died in 323 BCE, about 2,300 years ago, when he was not yet thirty-three, and his generals quarrelled and divided the empire. Greek cities, language and ideas remained in the East for centuries as a legacy of his conquests.

Ashoka ruled most of India about 2,300 years ago, and he won a terrible war in the east of the country in which many thousands of people died. Afterwards he is said to have felt deep sorrow, and he turned towards Buddhism and had messages about kindness, tolerance and fairness carved on stone pillars across his empire. Some of the pillars still stand today, and they are among the oldest royal messages that people can still read.

In 221 BCE China was united under the First Emperor, who introduced one writing system, one kind of money and one set of weights and measures for all his lands. He was buried near the city of Xi'an with an army of thousands of life-sized clay soldiers, discovered by farmers digging a well in 1974. Visitors notice that the faces of the figures differ from one another, as though each soldier had been modelled on a real person.

The Han dynasty followed the short-lived Qin, and it kept China united for about 400 years with a large army, a skilled civil service and good roads. By about 2,000 years ago, Chinese workers were making paper from rags, bark and old fishing nets, which was far cheaper than silk or bamboo strips. Paper would eventually carry knowledge and stories to every corner of the world, and it would outlast almost every other writing material.

Rome began as a small city beside the River Tiber, and over several centuries it grew until it ruled all the lands around the Mediterranean Sea. The Romans built about 80,000 kilometres of well-made roads, so that armies, officials, traders and messengers could travel quickly across the empire. Many modern highways still follow routes that were first laid out by Roman engineers.

The Romans built aqueducts to bring fresh water to their cities, as well as public baths, theatres and huge buildings made of concrete, some of which still survive. They also spread the Latin language, which became the ancestor of Spanish, French, Italian, Portuguese and Romanian. Roman law also left a deep mark on the legal systems of Europe and beyond.

Roman wealth depended heavily on slavery, and millions of people were captured, bought, sold and forced to work in homes, mines and fields. In 73 BCE a gladiator named Spartacus led a large revolt of enslaved people, which alarmed the whole empire for two years, but the Roman army finally crushed it. The story reminds us that the glories of ancient empires were built on the suffering of many.

Not every great state was in Europe or Asia, as the Maya and the kingdom of Aksum show. The Maya built stone cities with high temples, wrote in a complex script and followed a careful calendar in what is now Mexico and Central America. Aksum, in what is now Ethiopia, traded with Rome and India, and both civilisations flourished about 1,700 years ago, which shows that complex societies arose in many parts of the world.

Around 2,500 years ago, in different parts of the world, thinkers began to ask in a new way how people should live and what makes a good society. Confucius in China, the Buddha in India and Socrates in Greece all lived in this period, and their ideas spread widely, shaping much of later thought. Why so many great teachers appeared at about the same time is still debated, but growing cities and wars may have made people ask harder questions.

Confucius was a teacher who lived in China, and he taught that people should learn constantly, honour their families and rule with fairness and good example. His followers collected his sayings in a book called the Analects, which became the foundation of education and government in China for more than 2,000 years. He believed that a good society begins with the conduct of individuals, and that example matters far more than force or punishment.

The Buddha, whose name was Siddhartha Gautama, was born as a prince in northern India, and tradition says that the sight of suffering led him to leave his palace and search for wisdom. He taught that people can find peace through understanding, self-control and compassion, and Buddhism spread slowly across Asia along the trade routes. Today Buddhism has hundreds of millions of followers, and its teachings on peace and mindfulness are known far beyond Asia.

In Athens, about 2,500 years ago, citizens met in the open air to decide laws and policies themselves, which was a startling new idea in a world of kings. However, women, enslaved people and foreigners were not counted as citizens, so most of the people living in the city had no vote at all. The word democracy comes from Greek, but the Athenian version was far from complete.

Several of the world's great faiths grew from ancient roots that reach back about three thousand years or more, long before the age of empires. The Hebrew Bible records the belief in one God and the history of the Jewish people, while the Vedas, the oldest Hindu hymns, were spoken aloud and memorised for centuries before they were written down. Such traditions shaped the daily lives of millions, giving them festivals, laws and stories to live by.

Christianity began about 2,000 years ago in the Roman Empire, and it is based on the life and teachings of Jesus of Nazareth. It spread first among ordinary people, who were drawn by its message of love and forgiveness, and in spite of periods of persecution it had become one of the largest religions in the empire by the fourth century. Today it has about two billion followers, and it is found in almost every country on Earth, in many different forms.

Islam began in Arabia about 1,400 years ago, when Muhammad began to teach in Mecca the words that Muslims believe were revealed to him and are recorded in the Quran. Within a hundred years its followers had spread from Spain in the west to the borders of India in the east, and a great civilisation grew up under Islamic rulers. Today about a quarter of the world's people are Muslims, and the faith is followed on every continent in a wide variety of cultures.

Faiths travelled along trade routes with merchants, monks and pilgrims, and they gave people shared stories, rules and festivals, even across great distances. They often taught charity and care for strangers, and so helped communities to cooperate beyond the circle of family. At the same time, religious differences have also been a cause of conflict and suffering, and honest history must record both.

From about 2,100 years ago, roads and sea routes linked China with the Mediterranean, and in the nineteenth century a German geographer gave them the name Silk Road. Along them, traders carried silk, spices, glass, paper and ideas from one end of Asia to the other, but they also carried diseases. Few people ever travelled the whole distance, since goods usually passed through the hands of many different traders along the way.

Sailors learned that the monsoon winds blow in one direction for half the year and in the opposite direction for the rest. Using them, traders crossed the Indian Ocean regularly in wooden ships with triangular sails, linking Arabia, India, East Africa and China. Cities along the coast of East Africa grew rich on this trade in gold, ivory, cloth and spices.

In Baghdad, about 1,200 years ago, scholars of many faiths and nationalities gathered in a House of Wisdom and translated Greek, Persian and Indian books into Arabic. They did not simply copy what they found but added new ideas of their own in mathematics, astronomy and medicine. Without their care, many works of the ancient world might have been lost for ever.

Mathematicians in India treated zero as a true number with its own rules, and scholars in Baghdad spread the idea far beyond India. One of them, al-Khwarizmi, wrote a famous book on solving equations, and his work gave us the words algebra and algorithm. When the nine digits and zero reached Europe, they made calculation much easier than it had been with Roman numerals.

About 1,000 years ago the scholar Ibn al-Haytham tested how light and sight work by doing experiments, which was a new and powerful way to find the truth. The doctor Ibn Sina wrote a vast medical encyclopaedia that was studied in Asia and Europe for hundreds of years. Both men show that the habit of testing ideas is far older than modern science.

Chinese inventors made paper, printed books, gunpowder and the magnetic compass long before any of them reached Europe. The earliest dated printed book, a Buddhist text called the Diamond Sutra, was produced in China in the year 868, and sailors began to use the compass at sea about 900 years ago. Each of these inventions would eventually transform the way people in the West lived and fought.

In 1324 Mansa Musa, the king of Mali in West Africa, made a famous pilgrimage to Mecca with so much gold that prices rose in Cairo. His kingdom had grown rich from gold and salt, and under his rule the city of Timbuktu became a centre of books, teaching and trade. News of his wealth reached Europe, and mapmakers began to draw him on their maps.

In the Andes, the Inca ruled a huge empire by means of stone roads, relay runners and knotted cords called quipu, which recorded numbers and perhaps other information. In Mexico, the Aztec built Tenochtitlan on an island in a lake, with causeways, canals and floating gardens, and it became one of the largest cities in the world. Both empires were at the height of their power in the early 1500s, shortly before the first Europeans arrived on their shores.

Polynesian sailors crossed the vast Pacific Ocean in double canoes, finding their way by the stars, the swell of the waves and the flight of birds. They reached Hawaii, Easter Island and New Zealand, which was one of the last large lands to be settled by people, perhaps about 750 years ago. These were among the greatest feats of navigation in history, achieved without a compass or a map.

The Vikings came from Scandinavia and raided, traded and settled across Europe from about the year 800, travelling in fast and shallow longships. Some of them sailed to Iceland and Greenland, and about 1,000 years ago a few even reached Newfoundland in North America, where archaeologists have found the remains of a small camp. They were in the Americas almost 500 years before Columbus, but they did not stay.

In medieval Europe, most people were poor farmers who lived in villages and owed work or rent to a local lord. Monasteries kept the old books safe by copying them carefully by hand, and the first universities opened in places such as Bologna and Oxford during the 1100s. Learning grew slowly but steadily, helped by farming improvements such as the heavy plough that fed more people and freed some of them for other work.

In the 1200s the Mongols, under Genghis Khan and his family, built the largest land empire in history, stretching from Korea to Eastern Europe. They destroyed many cities, including Baghdad in 1258, but they also kept the roads safe for merchants and travellers, and ideas and inventions moved across Asia more freely than before. Their conquests also had a consequence that nobody at the time could have predicted, and it would travel along those same roads within a hundred years.

The Black Death was caused by a bacterium that lived in fleas, which in turn lived on rats, and it spread from Asia along the trade routes. In 1347 it reached Europe on ships that had come from the Black Sea, and within months the disease was moving through the ports of Italy. People who lived in crowded towns, with plenty of rats and little cleanliness, were especially at risk.

Between 1347 and 1351, the Black Death swept across Europe, and it may have killed a third or more of all the people on the continent. It also struck the Middle East and North Africa, and whole villages were left empty, their fields untended and their houses silent. It was one of the greatest disasters in human history, and it returned in smaller waves for centuries.

With so many workers dead, the survivors could demand higher pay, and landowners had little choice but to pay them. In western Europe, many peasants gained more freedom as a result, although in England a great revolt in 1381 showed how angry ordinary people still were at the rules that held them down. Terrible as it was, the plague changed the balance between rich and poor, and it showed that a society's workers hold real bargaining power.

People did not understand germs, so they argued about the cause, and some blamed innocent groups, especially Jewish communities, who were cruelly attacked in many towns. Some port cities, such as Dubrovnik, ordered ships to wait for thirty days, and later forty, before the crews could land, and this gave us the word quarantine, from the Italian for forty. It was a practical idea that helped, even though nobody could yet explain why.

In the Italian cities of the 1400s, rich merchants and bankers paid artists, architects and scholars to make their cities beautiful. This led to the Renaissance, a rebirth of art and of interest in the learning of Greece and Rome, and painters such as Leonardo da Vinci learned to show depth and light in new ways. Curiosity about the world, and about the human body and mind, became fashionable among the rich and the learned, and it would soon spread much further.

Between 1405 and 1433, the Chinese admiral Zheng He led seven great voyages with hundreds of ships, some of them far larger than any in Europe at the time. His fleets reached India, Arabia and East Africa, carrying silk and porcelain and bringing back gifts from foreign rulers. Afterwards, however, the Chinese court chose to end such expeditions, and the ships were allowed to decay.

About 1450 a goldsmith named Johannes Gutenberg built a printing press in the German city of Mainz, using small metal letters that could be arranged in any order and used again and again. Until then, every book had to be copied by hand, which made books rare and very costly. His most famous work, the Gutenberg Bible, was printed around 1455, and about fifty copies of it survive in libraries around the world today.

Printing with movable type was not invented only once, since Korean printers used metal type in 1377 and Chinese printers used clay type about 1040. In Europe, however, the alphabet has few letters, which suited the system well, and the press itself was based on machines that were already used for making wine and olive oil. Together with cheap paper, these advantages helped printing to spread quickly across Europe, and within fifty years there were presses in more than two hundred towns.

By 1500, millions of books had been printed in Europe, and printing helped ideas to spread faster than ever before. When Martin Luther criticised some practices of the Church in 1517, his writings were printed and read all over Germany within weeks, and the result was a split in European Christianity. Literacy increased as books became cheaper, and ordinary people began to read for themselves.

In 1453 the Ottoman army used huge cannons to break the walls of Constantinople, the great city that had stood as the capital of the eastern Roman Empire for a thousand years. After this, gunpowder weapons changed how wars were fought, since castles could no longer protect their lords and rulers needed large sums of money to buy cannons. The age of knights in armour was ending, and the age of states with great armies was beginning.

In the 1400s sailors from Portugal explored the west coast of Africa in small, nimble ships called caravels, which could sail close to the wind. They used compasses, improved maps and an instrument called the astrolabe, and they hoped to find a sea route to the spices and gold of Asia. Step by step they pushed farther south, and each voyage taught them something about the winds and currents of the Atlantic.

In 1498 the Portuguese captain Vasco da Gama sailed around the southern tip of Africa and reached the port of Calicut in India, after a voyage that had lasted about ten months. This sea route let Europeans trade directly with Asia, without paying the merchants who controlled the old land routes, and it brought great profits to Portugal. Armed ships and fortified trading posts soon followed along the coasts of Africa and Asia, as Portugal tried to control the trade in spices.

In 1492 Christopher Columbus, who was sailing for the rulers of Spain, crossed the Atlantic Ocean and landed on an island in the Bahamas. He believed that he had reached the edge of Asia, but in fact he had come to a continent where millions of people already lived, and where they had lived for at least 15,000 years. His voyages, and those of the explorers who followed him, began a lasting contact between the two halves of the world that has never been broken.

In 1519 a Spanish fleet led by Ferdinand Magellan set out to find a western route to the spice islands of Asia. Magellan was killed in a battle in the Philippines in 1521, and only one of the five ships and about 18 men returned to Spain in 1522, after sailing right around the world. The journey proved beyond doubt that the Earth is round and that all its oceans are connected.

After 1492, crops, animals and diseases began to cross the oceans in both directions, in a process that historians call the Columbian exchange. It changed what people ate and how they lived in every continent, and it linked separate parts of the world into a single web of life. But it also brought terrible suffering to the Americas, as the next pages describe.

Potatoes, maize, tomatoes, chillies and chocolate went from the Americas to the rest of the world, and they helped to feed more people in Europe, Africa and Asia. Horses, cattle, wheat, sugar and sheep went the other way, and horses transformed life on the grasslands of North America. Italian food without tomatoes, or Indian food without chillies, would have been unrecognisable before this exchange.

In 1521 a small Spanish army led by Hernán Cortés, with the help of thousands of local allies and a deadly outbreak of smallpox, overthrew the Aztec empire in Mexico. About ten years later Francisco Pizarro and a few hundred men took over the Inca empire in Peru, which had been weakened by civil war and disease. Many of the peoples who joined the invaders had been ruled harshly by the Aztec and Inca, and hoped for freedom.

In 1545 Spanish miners found a mountain of silver at Potosí, in what is now Bolivia, and the town grew to be one of the largest cities in the world. The silver was shipped to Europe and across the Pacific to China, where it was in great demand, so for the first time money from one continent paid for goods on another. The work in the mines was brutal, and many local people were forced to do it.

From the 1500s to the 1800s, more than 10 million people were taken from Africa and forced to work as slaves in the Americas, and many more died during the capture and the voyage. They grew sugar, cotton and tobacco on plantations, and the trade made many European merchants wealthy while it destroyed African families and communities. The memory of this cruelty remains painful to millions of their descendants today, and its effects can still be seen in many societies.

In 1602 the Dutch East India Company sold shares to the public, which allowed ordinary people to own a part of a trading business and share in its profits. Companies like this had their own ships, forts and soldiers, and they became powerful players in global trade, sometimes ruling whole territories. They also invented new ways of raising money that we still use in stock markets today.

In 1543 a Polish scholar named Nicolaus Copernicus published the idea that the Earth moves around the Sun, instead of the Sun around the Earth. This challenged the old belief, held for centuries and supported by great authorities, that the Earth stood still at the centre of everything. The book appeared in the year he died, so he never had to face the storm that it caused.

From the 1500s a new way of finding out spread across Europe, based on careful observation and experiment rather than on the authority of ancient books. In 1610 Galileo used a telescope to see four moons moving around Jupiter, which showed that not everything in the heavens circled the Earth. His discoveries made him famous throughout Italy, but they also earned him some powerful enemies among scholars and churchmen who disagreed.

In 1633 a Church court forced Galileo to say that the Earth does not move, because its judges believed that his ideas went against the Bible. He spent the rest of his life under house arrest, but his books continued to be read, and the questions he asked could not be silenced. The story is often told as a battle between science and religion, although the truth was more complicated.

The microscope, invented in the early 1600s, opened up a hidden world that nobody had known before. In 1665 Robert Hooke looked at a thin slice of cork and named the tiny boxes that he saw cells, and soon afterwards Antonie van Leeuwenhoek discovered swarms of tiny living creatures in a drop of pond water. Until then, no one had even suspected that such tiny forms of life existed, let alone that they filled every drop of water.

In 1687 Isaac Newton published a great book showing how a single law of gravity explains why an apple falls and why the Moon circles the Earth. It suggested that the same simple laws work everywhere in the universe, and that the universe is something people can understand with mathematics. For the next two hundred years scientists worked inside the framework that he had built.

Scientists began to share their work in societies and journals, such as the Royal Society of London, founded in 1660, where others could test and correct it. Science grew because people were willing to admit when they were wrong, and because a claim had to be supported by evidence and not merely by the rank of the person who made it. That habit of honest doubt turned out to be an extraordinarily powerful tool, and it remains the core of how science works today.

In the 1700s writers in Europe argued for reason, free speech and human rights, and this period is known as the Enlightenment. Their ideas inspired the American Revolution of 1776 and the French Revolution of 1789, and later struggles for freedom and equality all over the world. The promise of those ideals was far greater than their practice, because they were not at first applied to women or to enslaved people.

In the late 1700s a movement to end the slave trade grew in Britain, led by religious groups and by former slaves such as Olaudah Equiano, who wrote a book about his life. Britain banned the trade in 1807 and ended slavery in its empire in 1833, while the United States ended it in 1865 after a terrible civil war. Enslaved people themselves played a major part, from the Haitian Revolution to countless smaller acts of resistance.

In 1859 Charles Darwin published On the Origin of Species, which explained how living things change over time through a process of natural selection. He showed that all living things, including humans, share common ancestors, and the idea changed biology for ever, although it also provoked fierce arguments that have not yet entirely died away. Modern studies of DNA have confirmed his main conclusion in remarkable detail, including the close family link between humans and the other apes.

Women were often shut out of universities and learned societies, but many of them contributed to science in spite of this. Maria Sibylla Merian travelled to Suriname to paint and study insects in the early 1700s, and Émilie du Châtelet translated Newton's great work into French and explained it clearly to a wider audience. Their stories remind us that the history of knowledge has always had more contributors than the textbooks admit.

From about 1760, Britain began to use coal, steam engines and machines in large factories on a scale never seen before. The cotton industry grew astonishingly fast, and many people left the countryside to find work in the new towns, in a change that historians call the Industrial Revolution. It began in a small corner of Europe, but its effects soon reached the whole world.

Coal is energy that was stored by plants millions of years ago, and burning it releases that energy as heat. Steam engines turned this heat into movement, and they did work that once needed the muscles of many people and animals, which James Watt greatly improved in the 1760s and 1770s. For the first time in history, human societies were no longer limited by how much muscle power they could gather.

Cities grew at an astonishing speed, and by about 1800 London had more than a million people, a number not seen in Europe since ancient Rome. Many streets were crowded and dirty, and diseases such as cholera spread easily where there was no clean drinking water. The old cities were bursting with newcomers, and nobody knew how to manage such numbers.

Factory work was long and hard, with machines that ran without rest, and children worked in mills and mines for very little money. Over many years, new laws and workers' unions slowly improved conditions, and in time wages began to rise as workers became more skilled. The progress came because ordinary people demanded it, not because the owners offered it.

In the 1800s, railways made travel much faster than a horse could, and the first passenger railway opened in England in 1825. Trains carried people, food, coal and goods across whole countries, towns near the stations grew rich, and the railway companies even insisted on a single standard time so that their timetables made sense. A journey that had once taken several days by coach could now be completed in a few hours, and ordinary families could travel for pleasure.

The telegraph sent messages along wires in moments, and it was first used in 1844 with the dots and dashes of Samuel Morse's code. After some early failures, a lasting cable crossed the Atlantic Ocean in 1866, so news from America reached Europe in minutes instead of weeks. The world began to feel smaller and busier, and the pace of business and politics quickened.

Electricity changed homes and factories alike, and practical electric lamps appeared in the 1870s, after earlier experiments by scientists such as Michael Faraday. Soon cities had power stations and telephones, and the evening hours were no longer ruled by the dark. Today almost every machine we use, from a kettle to a hospital scanner, depends on this invisible force, and most of us rarely give it a thought.

In 1885 Karl Benz built one of the first petrol cars in Germany, and the engine drove a tiny three-wheeled vehicle. Henry Ford's moving assembly line, which began in 1913, made cars so cheap that ordinary families could buy them, and it changed the shape of cities and the pattern of daily life. Roads, suburbs, petrol stations and oil wells followed the car all over the world, and so did the traffic jams and the pollution.

The human population passed one billion about 1800, a figure that had taken our species hundreds of thousands of years to reach. After that, growth became faster and faster, with two billion by 1927, four billion by 1974 and eight billion in 2022. No other large animal has multiplied so quickly, and it was the new energy, food and medicine of the modern age that made it possible.

By 1914 European states ruled most of Africa and large parts of Asia, and they usually did not ask the people who lived there. These empires took raw materials, sold their own factory goods and sometimes forced people to work, and many peoples resisted them, in ways ranging from petitions to rebellions. The lines drawn on maps in this period still shape the borders of many countries today.
