For most of history, large numbers of children perished in infancy, and the average span of life was short as a consequence. In about 1800 more than four in ten children died before their fifth birthday, whereas today the figure is about four in a hundred, one of the most remarkable improvements in human history. Parents of earlier centuries lived with a dread that most families today scarcely know.

In 1796 an English doctor named Edward Jenner showed that people who caught a mild illness called cowpox did not catch smallpox, which was far deadlier. He used this discovery to make the first vaccine, and the word itself comes from the Latin word for cow. Similar methods had been known in parts of Asia and Africa before, but Jenner's work spread widely.

Smallpox killed hundreds of millions of people over the centuries, and many survivors were left scarred or blind. After a worldwide campaign of vaccination, in which health workers travelled to the remotest villages, the disease was wiped out by 1980, and it is still the only human disease to have been removed completely. It was a rare and splendid victory of cooperation between rich and poor countries, achieved even at a time when the world's great powers were bitter rivals.

In the 1800s doctors began to discover that tiny living things called germs cause many diseases. Ignaz Semmelweis showed that washing hands saved mothers' lives in hospital, John Snow traced a cholera outbreak to a single London water pump, and later Louis Pasteur and Robert Koch proved the germ theory. Understanding the cause of a disease is the first step towards preventing it, and the germ theory gave doctors that understanding at last.

Clean water and sewers did more to save lives than almost any medicine, because they stopped diseases such as cholera and typhoid from spreading. After a terrible smell rose from the River Thames in 1858, London built a huge sewer system under its streets, and cities all over the world copied it. Hardly anybody thinks of these buried pipes when they praise the wonders of modern medicine, yet they have saved countless lives.

In 1928 Alexander Fleming noticed that a mould had killed the bacteria around it in a dish in his laboratory, and he reported his discovery. Other scientists made it into the drug penicillin, which was produced in large amounts during the Second World War, and antibiotics now cure many infections that once killed. Some germs are learning to resist them, however, so these drugs must be used with care.

In the early 1900s two German chemists, Fritz Haber and Carl Bosch, found a way to make fertiliser from nitrogen in the air, a method that is still used today. Many experts think that about half of the people alive today eat food that was grown with it, which means that the invention has quietly shaped the lives of billions. The process also uses a great deal of energy, and the excess fertiliser that washes off fields can pollute rivers and seas.

In the 1960s the scientist Norman Borlaug and his colleagues bred short, strong wheat that gave far bigger harvests, and farmers grew it widely in Mexico, India and Pakistan. Many experts believe that this green revolution saved millions of people from hunger, though it also required large amounts of water and chemicals. Famines still happen, but they are now more often caused by war and politics than by a simple shortage of food in the world as a whole.

Over the past 200 years life has improved in many ways for a great number of people. In 1820 about eight in ten people lived in extreme poverty, but today fewer than one in ten do, according to one widely used measure, although hundreds of millions are still very poor. Progress of this kind was never automatic, and it was won by ordinary people working for change.

As more children survived, and as women gained education and rights, parents began to have fewer children, first in Europe and North America and later in much of the world. Families grew smaller, and the growth of the world's population began to slow, even though the total is still rising. Many countries now worry about having too few children rather than too many, as their populations grow older and begin to shrink.

The First World War, from 1914 to 1918, was the first great war fought with weapons made in huge factories, such as machine guns, heavy artillery and poison gas. About ten million soldiers and many millions of civilians died, and the old empires of Germany, Austria, Russia and Turkey fell. The peace that followed proved fragile, and it left bitter feelings that would lead to another war.

In 1918 and 1919 a flu pandemic spread around the world on ships and trains, while the war was ending and soldiers were travelling home. Scientists estimate that about 50 million people died, which was more than the war itself, and it struck young adults especially hard. Most countries had no vaccines or antibiotics at that time, so doctors could only try to relieve the sickness.

The Second World War, from 1939 to 1945, killed tens of millions of people and was the deadliest war in history, and most of the dead were civilians. Six million Jews, along with many other people, were murdered by Nazi Germany in a planned campaign of hatred called the Holocaust. It is a warning of what can happen when a state turns prejudice into policy.

In 1945 the first atomic bombs were used on two cities in Japan, and the war ended soon afterwards, after enormous loss of life. Since then nuclear weapons have become far more powerful, and the fear of a nuclear war was a part of life for decades during the Cold War between the United States and the Soviet Union. Remarkably, no nuclear weapon has been used in war since the summer of 1945, although the danger has never entirely gone away.

In 1945 the United Nations was founded to help keep the peace, and in 1948 it published the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, a list of rights that belong to every person. After the war many colonies became independent, starting with India in 1947 and many African countries in the 1960s, and the age of European empires came to an end. Not every promise was kept, and many people still wait for their rights, but the principle had at least been set down for all to see.

In 1903 two brothers, Wilbur and Orville Wright, made the first powered flight in a small aeroplane on a windy beach at Kitty Hawk in the United States. It lasted only twelve seconds and covered about thirty-seven metres, but within a lifetime jet planes were carrying millions of people across oceans in a few hours. Distances that had once taken weeks of hard travel by sea were now crossed in a single day, with time to spare before dinner.

In 1957 the Soviet Union launched Sputnik, the first satellite to orbit the Earth, and the little silver ball startled the world as it beeped overhead. In 1961 Yuri Gagarin travelled once around the Earth in a spacecraft, and he became the first person in space after a flight of less than two hours. It began a famous race into space between the Soviet Union and the United States, which pushed both sides to invent new machines at great speed.

In July 1969 the American spacecraft Apollo 11 landed on the Moon, and Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin walked on its dusty grey surface while hundreds of millions of people watched on television. Only 66 years had passed since the first short flight of the Wright brothers, and many people living at the time had seen both events. It was the first time that human beings had set foot on another world.

In 1968 astronauts in orbit around the Moon took a famous photograph of the Earth rising above the bare grey surface, a blue and white ball against black space. The picture showed how small and fragile our planet is, and it helped to inspire the first Earth Day in 1970 and the growth of the environmental movement. Many people saw their home for the first time as a single place, with no borders visible, and with limits that no one could ignore.

The first computers filled whole rooms and needed teams of people to run them, but after the invention of the transistor and then the microchip, they became smaller, faster and much cheaper. The World Wide Web, invented by Tim Berners-Lee, began about 1990, and today more than five billion people use the internet, many of them on phones that are far more powerful than those early machines. Few changes in the long history of humankind have spread around the world so quickly, or have altered so many ordinary habits.

Burning coal, oil and gas adds carbon dioxide to the air, and this gas traps heat in the atmosphere, much like a blanket around the Earth. Since the 1800s the planet has warmed by a little more than one degree Celsius, and the air now holds about half as much carbon dioxide again as it did then. This is a larger and faster change than any that our species has met before in its long history.

A warmer world brings stronger heat waves, longer droughts and heavier floods, and the sea is slowly rising as the ice on land melts. In 2015 nearly every country agreed in Paris to try to limit the warming, but many scientists say that much more must be done, and quickly. The cost of change is great, but so is the cost of doing nothing.

Humans and the animals that we keep for food, such as cattle and pigs, now make up most of the weight of all the mammals on Earth. Wild mammals are only a small fraction of the total, and many wild species are in danger as forests are cut down and their homes shrink. This is the most dramatic change that our species has brought to the living world.

The last passenger pigeon, a bird that was once among the most numerous in North America and flew in flocks that darkened the sky, died in a zoo in 1914. Scientists warn that up to a million species of plants and animals may be at risk of dying out, many of them within a few decades, unless we act. Every species that is lost is a story that can never be told again, and the loss also makes the whole web of life less secure.

People can solve shared problems when they decide to work together, even when their interests seem to pull in different directions. In 1987 a world treaty stopped the use of chemicals that were damaging the ozone layer, which protects life from harmful rays, and in 1986 most commercial whale hunting was banned, so some whales are slowly returning. These successes prove that real agreement among nations is possible, and that the damage done by people can sometimes be repaired by people.

Energy from the sun and the wind has become much cheaper in the past fifteen years, and in many places it is now the cheapest way to make electricity. Many countries are building more solar panels and wind farms each year, which gives hope of using less coal, oil and gas in the future. Technology has often created our problems, but it can also help to solve them.

In 2003 scientists finished reading the full human genome, the complete set of instructions in our DNA, after a project that took thirteen years and many nations. They found that any two people are almost exactly the same, differing in only about one letter in a thousand, so the differences between us are tiny compared with what we share. That fact is, in many ways, the deepest scientific answer to the question of who we are, and it holds true whatever our nationality or colour.

New tools, such as gene editing and artificial intelligence, give people great power, and they have the potential to do much good, from treating diseases to speeding up research. Societies must decide how to use them wisely and fairly, and ordinary people, and not only experts and companies, have a part in those choices. Nobody can yet say how that story will turn out, because the outcome will depend on the choices that people make from now on.

Humans took over the world not because we were the strongest or the fastest, but because we learned to share what we know. Language, writing, trade, science and the internet let each generation build on the work of the last, and so knowledge grew faster than any single mind could manage. From the first campfire to the screens in our pockets, the secret has always been cooperation.

All people alive today belong to a single species, and our DNA is almost exactly the same, whatever country we come from or language we speak. We took over the world not because we were the strongest, but because we learned to share what we know, from the first spoken word to the latest discovery. What happens in the next chapter will depend on whether we can use that knowledge with care, for each other and for the planet that we all share.
